The convention a⁰ = 1 keeps all exponent rules consistent. Note: 0⁰ is considered indeterminate in some contexts, though it's conventionally defined as 1 in combinatorics and computer science.

faq.question: What does a negative exponent mean?
faq.answer: A negative exponent means 'take the reciprocal': a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Examples: 10⁻¹ = 0.1, 2⁻³ = 1/8, 5⁻² = 1/25. In scientific notation: 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.00035. Negative exponents represent very small numbers.

faq.question: What is scientific notation?
faq.answer: Scientific notation expresses numbers as a coefficient (1–10) times a power of 10. Examples: 6,380,000 = 6.38 × 10⁶; 0.00042 = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴. It makes very large and very small numbers readable. The exponent tells you how many places to move the decimal point (positive = right/large, negative = left/small).

definition: A value that, when multiplied by itself, gives the original number. The square root of 25 is 5 because 5 × 5 = 25.
contentHTML:
What is a Square Root?

The square root of a number x is a value y such that y² = x. Written as √x or x^(1/2). For example, √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. Every positive number has two square roots (positive and negative), but √ conventionally refers to the positive (principal) root.

Perfect Squares Reference

√nn√nn
√1 = 11√121 = 11121
√4 = 24√144 = 12144
√9 = 39√169 = 13169
√16 = 416√196 = 14196
√25 = 525√225 = 15225
√36 = 636√256 = 16256
√49 = 749√289 = 17289
√64 = 864√324 = 18324
√81 = 981√400 = 20400
√100 = 10100√625 = 25625

Square Root Properties

  • √(a × b) = √a × √b → √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2
  • √(a / b) = √a / √b → √(9/16) = 3/4
  • √a² = |a| (always positive)
  • Square root of a negative number is imaginary: √(-1) = i

faq.question: What is the square root of a negative number?
faq.answer: In real numbers, negative numbers have no square root (no real number squared gives a negative). In the complex number system, √(-1) = i (the 'imaginary unit'). √(-9) = 3i, √(-16) = 4i. Complex numbers (a + bi) are essential in electrical engineering, quantum mechanics, and signal processing.

faq.question: How do I simplify square roots?
faq.answer: Factor out perfect squares: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. √200 = √(100 × 2) = 10√2. √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3. Find the largest perfect square factor, take its root outside, and leave the remainder under the radical.

faq.question: Is √2 a rational or irrational number?
faq.answer: √2 is irrational — it cannot be expressed as a fraction of two integers. Its decimal expansion is non-terminating and non-repeating: 1.41421356... This was proven by the ancient Greeks (proof by contradiction). Most square roots of non-perfect-squares are irrational: √3, √5, √7, etc.

definition: The mathematical constant approximately equal to 3.14159, representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
contentHTML:
What is Pi (π)?

Pi (π) is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately equal to 3.14159265358979.... It is an irrational, transcendental number — its decimal expansion never terminates or repeats. Pi is one of the most important constants in mathematics, appearing in geometry, trigonometry, physics, engineering, and statistics.

Key Formulas Using π

FormulaWhat It Calculates
C = πd = 2πrCircumference of a circle
A = πr²Area of a circle
V = (4/3)πr³Volume of a sphere
SA = 4πr²Surface area of a sphere
V = πr²hVolume of a cylinder
A = πabArea of an ellipse

Pi Approximations

ApproximationValueAccuracy
33.000~4.5% error
22/73.142857...~0.04% error
355/1133.14159292...~0.000008% error (best fraction under 1000)
3.141595 decimalsSufficient for most calculations

Pi in Nature and Engineering

  • Normal distribution: The bell curve formula includes 1/√(2π)
  • Euler's identity: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 — connecting the 5 most important constants
  • GPS and navigation: Pi in spherical geometry calculations
  • Electrical engineering: AC waveforms use 2πf (angular frequency)

faq.question: How many digits of pi do I need?
faq.answer: For virtually all practical purposes, 3.14159 (5 digits) is sufficient. NASA uses 15 digits for interplanetary navigation. With 39 digits, you can calculate the circumference of the observable universe to the accuracy of a single hydrogen atom. As of 2024, pi has been calculated to 105 trillion digits — purely for mathematical interest and computing benchmarks.

faq.question: Why is pi irrational?
faq.answer: Pi cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers — its decimal never repeats or terminates. This was proven by Johann Heinrich Lambert in 1761. It's also transcendental (proven by Ferdinand von Lindemann in 1882), meaning it's not the root of any polynomial with rational coefficients. This proves the ancient problem of 'squaring the circle' with compass and straightedge is impossible.

faq.question: What is the difference between π and τ (tau)?
faq.answer: τ (tau) = 2π ≈ 6.28318. Some mathematicians argue τ is more natural because it represents a full revolution (360°), while π is a half revolution (180°). With τ: circumference = τr, full circle = τ radians. The τ vs π debate is ongoing in math education, but π remains the universal standard in science, engineering, and computing.

definition: A fundamental theorem in geometry stating that in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a² + b² = c².
contentHTML:
What is the Pythagorean Theorem?

The Pythagorean Theorem states that in any right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides:

a² + b² = c²

This is arguably the most well-known and widely applied theorem in all of mathematics, fundamental to geometry, trigonometry, physics, engineering, and navigation.

Solving for Each Side

FindFormulaExample (a=3, b=4)
Hypotenuse (c)c = √(a² + b²)c = √(9+16) = √25 = 5
Leg (a)a = √(c² − b²)a = √(25−16) = √9 = 3
Leg (b)b = √(c² − a²)b = √(25−9) = √16 = 4

Common Pythagorean Triples

abcMultiples
3456-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20
5121310-24-26, 15-36-39
8151716-30-34
7242514-48-50

Real-World Applications

  • Construction: The 3-4-5 rule checks if corners are square (90°)
  • Navigation: Distance between two GPS coordinates
  • Screen size: 16" wide × 9" tall = √(256+81) = √337 ≈ 18.4" diagonal
  • Ladder safety: 12' ladder against a wall, base 3' out → reaches √(144−9) = √135 ≈ 11.6' high

faq.question: Does the Pythagorean Theorem work for all triangles?
faq.answer: No — only for RIGHT triangles (containing a 90° angle). For non-right triangles, use the Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos(C), which reduces to a² + b² = c² when angle C = 90° (since cos(90°) = 0). However, the Pythagorean relationship can TEST if a triangle is right-angled: if a²+b² = c², it's a right triangle.

faq.question: What is the 3-4-5 rule in construction?
faq.answer: The 3-4-5 rule uses the Pythagorean triple (3,4,5) to verify a corner is exactly 90°. Measure 3 feet along one wall, 4 feet along the other, and if the diagonal is exactly 5 feet, the corner is square. Carpenters also use multiples: 6-8-10 or 9-12-15 for larger projects. It's the simplest, most reliable method for checking right angles on a job site.

faq.question: How do I find the distance between two points?
faq.answer: The distance formula IS the Pythagorean theorem applied to coordinates: d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). For 3D: d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²). Example: distance from (1,2) to (4,6) = √((3)² + (4)²) = √(9+16) = √25 = 5.

definition: A second-degree polynomial equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, solvable using the quadratic formula: x = (-b ± √(b²-4ac)) / 2a.
contentHTML:
What is a Quadratic Equation?

A quadratic equation is a second-degree polynomial equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. It produces a parabola when graphed. Every quadratic equation has exactly two solutions (which may be real or complex, and may be equal).

The Quadratic Formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a

The Discriminant (Δ = b² − 4ac)

Discriminant ValueMeaningGraph
Δ > 0Two distinct real solutionsParabola crosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0One repeated real solutionParabola touches x-axis once (vertex)
Δ < 0Two complex conjugate solutionsParabola doesn't cross x-axis

Solving Methods

MethodBest ForExample: x² − 5x + 6 = 0
FactoringSimple integer solutions(x−2)(x−3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3
Quadratic FormulaAny quadratic equationx = (5 ± √(25−24))/2 = (5±1)/2 → 2 or 3
Completing the SquareDeriving vertex form(x − 5/2)² = 1/4 → x = 5/2 ± 1/2

Real-World Applications

  • Projectile motion: h(t) = −16t² + v₀t + h₀ (height as function of time)
  • Business: Profit = −ax² + bx − c (profit maximization at vertex)
  • Engineering: Cable sag, arch design, trajectory calculations
  • Physics: Kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion

faq.question: What does the discriminant tell you?
faq.answer: The discriminant (b² − 4ac) reveals the nature of solutions WITHOUT solving: Δ > 0 → two different real solutions; Δ = 0 → one repeated real solution (perfect square); Δ < 0 → two complex solutions (no real x-intercepts). Example: for 2x² + 3x + 5 = 0, Δ = 9 − 40 = −31 < 0, so this equation has no real solutions.

faq.question: How do I find the vertex of a parabola?
faq.answer: Vertex x-coordinate: x = −b/(2a). Plug back in to find y. For y = 2x² − 8x + 3: vertex x = 8/4 = 2, vertex y = 2(4) − 16 + 3 = −5. Vertex is (2, −5). If a > 0, the vertex is the minimum point; if a < 0, it's the maximum. The vertex form is y = a(x − h)² + k where (h,k) is the vertex.

faq.question: When should I use factoring vs the quadratic formula?
faq.answer: Try factoring first — it's fastest when solutions are small integers. If the equation doesn't factor easily (non-integer solutions or complex numbers), use the quadratic formula, which works for ALL quadratic equations. The formula is also necessary when Δ < 0 (complex solutions). Pro tip: always check the discriminant first to know what type of solutions to expect.

definition: An ordered arrangement of objects. The number of permutations of n objects taken r at a time is P(n,r) = n! / (n-r)!.
contentHTML:
What is a Permutation?

A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects. The number of permutations of n objects taken r at a time is the number of distinct sequences that can be formed. Order matters in permutations — ABC is different from BAC.

Permutation Formula

P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!

Examples

ProblemFormulaResult
Arrange 5 books on a shelfP(5,5) = 5!120 arrangements
Choose President, VP, Secretary from 10 peopleP(10,3) = 10!/7!720 ways
4-digit PIN (digits 0-9, no repeat)P(10,4) = 10!/6!5,040 codes
First 3 finishers in a 20-person raceP(20,3) = 20!/17!6,840 outcomes

Permutation vs Combination

FeaturePermutationCombination
OrderMatters (AB ≠ BA)Doesn't matter (AB = BA)
Formulan!/(n−r)!n!/(r!(n−r)!)
Choosing 3 from 56010
ExamplesRankings, PINs, seating chartsCommittees, lottery, teams

faq.question: What is the difference between permutation and combination?
faq.answer: Permutations count ordered arrangements (the sequence matters). Combinations count selections (order doesn't matter). Choosing a committee of 3 from 10 people is a combination (C(10,3)=120) because the committee {A,B,C} is the same as {C,B,A}. Electing President, VP, and Treasurer from 10 is a permutation (P(10,3)=720) because order matters.

faq.question: What is a permutation with repetition?
faq.answer: When objects can be reused, the formula changes to nʳ (n choices for each of r positions). A 4-digit PIN with digits 0-9 (repetition allowed) has 10⁴ = 10,000 possibilities. Without repetition it's P(10,4) = 5,040. Repetition dramatically increases the count.

faq.question: How do I calculate permutations of items with duplicates?
faq.answer: If some items are identical, divide by the factorial of each group of duplicates. For the letters in MISSISSIPPI (11 letters: 1M, 4I, 4S, 2P), the number of distinct arrangements = 11!/(4!×4!×2!) = 34,650. This avoids counting identical arrangements as different.

definition: A selection of objects where order does not matter. The number of combinations of n objects taken r at a time is C(n,r) = n! / (r!(n-r)!).
contentHTML:
What is a Combination?

A combination is a selection of objects where order does not matter. Choosing players A, B, C for a team is the same as choosing C, A, B — both are the same combination.

Combination Formula

C(n, r) = n! / (r! × (n − r)!)

Also written as "n choose r" or ⁿCᵣ or (n r)

Examples

ProblemFormulaResult
Choose 3 toppings from 8C(8,3) = 8!/(3!×5!)56 combinations
Lottery: 6 from 49C(49,6)13,983,816 (1 in 14 million odds)
Poker hand: 5 from 52C(52,5)2,598,960 hands
Team of 5 from 12 playersC(12,5)792 teams

Pascal's Triangle and Combinations

Pascal's Triangle gives C(n,r) values. Each entry is the sum of the two entries above it:

  • Row 0: 1
  • Row 1: 1 1
  • Row 2: 1 2 1
  • Row 3: 1 3 3 1
  • Row 4: 1 4 6 4 1
  • Row 5: 1 5 10 10 5 1

Row n, position r gives C(n,r). Example: Row 5, position 2 = 10 = C(5,2).

faq.question: When do I use combinations vs permutations?
faq.answer: Ask: 'Does the ORDER of selection matter?' If yes → permutation. If no → combination. Selecting a committee of 3: combination (the group {A,B,C} is the same regardless of selection order). Assigning 1st, 2nd, 3rd place: permutation (order matters). Choosing a password: permutation. Drawing lottery numbers: combination.

faq.question: What are the odds of winning the lottery?
faq.answer: For Powerball (5 from 69 + 1 from 26): C(69,5) × 26 = 292,201,338 combinations → odds of winning are 1 in 292.2 million. For Mega Millions (5 from 70 + 1 from 25): odds are 1 in 302.6 million. Smaller state lotteries have better odds: a Pick 6 from 49 has C(49,6) = 13,983,816 → 1 in 14 million.

faq.question: What is the binomial theorem?
faq.answer: The binomial theorem expands (a+b)ⁿ using combinations: (a+b)ⁿ = Σ C(n,k) × aⁿ⁻ᵏ × bᵏ for k=0 to n. The coefficients are the combinations C(n,k) — which are exactly the numbers in Pascal's Triangle. Example: (a+b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ (coefficients 1,3,3,1 = Row 3 of Pascal's).

definition: A measure of the likelihood that an event will occur, expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
contentHTML:
What is Probability?

Probability measures the likelihood of an event occurring, expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), or equivalently 0% to 100%. It is the foundation of statistics, risk analysis, gambling, insurance, and decision-making.

Basic Probability Formula

P(Event) = Number of favorable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes

Probability Scale

ProbabilityMeaningExample
0ImpossibleRolling a 7 on a standard die
0.01 (1%)Very unlikelyBeing struck by lightning in your life
0.25 (25%)UnlikelyDrawing a heart from a deck
0.50 (50%)Even chanceFlipping heads on a fair coin
0.75 (75%)LikelyNOT drawing a heart from a deck
0.99 (99%)Almost certainSun rising tomorrow
1CertainRolling 1-6 on a standard die

Key Probability Rules

RuleFormulaWhen
ComplementP(not A) = 1 − P(A)Probability of an event NOT happening
Addition (OR)P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)Either event occurring
Multiplication (AND)P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A)Both events occurring
Independent EventsP(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)Events don't affect each other

faq.question: What is the probability of rolling two sixes in a row?
faq.answer: Each die roll is independent. P(first six) = 1/6. P(second six) = 1/6. P(both) = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36 ≈ 2.78%. For three sixes: (1/6)³ = 1/216 ≈ 0.46%. The multiplication rule for independent events: multiply individual probabilities.

faq.question: What is conditional probability?
faq.answer: Conditional probability P(A|B) is the probability of A given that B has already occurred. Example: P(drawing a king | card is a face card) = 4/12 = 1/3 (12 face cards, 4 are kings). Bayes' Theorem relates conditional probabilities: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). This is fundamental to medical testing, spam filters, and machine learning.

faq.question: What is the gambler's fallacy?
faq.answer: The mistaken belief that past independent events affect future probabilities. After flipping 10 heads in a row, the probability of the next flip being heads is still exactly 50% — the coin has no memory. Each flip is independent. However, the probability of getting 11 heads in a row BEFORE you start is (1/2)¹¹ = 1/2048 — that's different from the probability of the next single flip.

definition: The measure of the two-dimensional space enclosed by a shape, expressed in square units (ft², m², etc.).
contentHTML:
What is Area?

Area is the measure of the two-dimensional space enclosed by a shape, expressed in square units (ft², m², in², cm², acres, hectares). It answers: "How much surface does this shape cover?"

Area Formulas for Common Shapes

ShapeFormulaExample
RectangleA = length × width10' × 12' = 120 ft²
SquareA = side²8' × 8' = 64 ft²
TriangleA = ½ × base × height½ × 10' × 6' = 30 ft²
CircleA = πr²π × 5² = 78.54 ft²
TrapezoidA = ½(b₁ + b₂) × h½(8+12) × 5 = 50 ft²
ParallelogramA = base × height10' × 7' = 70 ft²
EllipseA = π × a × bπ × 6 × 4 = 75.4 ft²

Area Unit Conversions

FromToMultiply By
1 ft²in²144
1 yd²ft²9
1 acreft²43,560
1 m²ft²10.764
1 hectareacres2.471
1 mi²acres640

faq.question: How do I calculate the area of an irregular shape?
faq.answer: Break the irregular shape into regular shapes (rectangles, triangles, circles), calculate each area, then add them together. For curved shapes, use the trapezoidal rule or Simpson's rule for approximation. In practice, apps and tools can calculate area from coordinates or Google Maps measurements. For land, surveyors use GPS and coordinate geometry.

faq.question: How many square feet is an acre?
faq.answer: 1 acre = 43,560 square feet. An acre is roughly the size of a football field (which is 48,000 sq ft including end zones, so an acre is about 91% of a football field). A standard residential lot in the US is typically 0.15–0.50 acres (6,500–21,800 sq ft).

faq.question: What is the difference between area and perimeter?
faq.answer: Area measures the space INSIDE a shape (in square units) — how much carpet to cover a room. Perimeter measures the distance AROUND a shape (in linear units) — how much fencing to go around a yard. A 10' × 20' room has area = 200 ft² and perimeter = 60 ft. They measure fundamentally different things.

definition: The measure of three-dimensional space occupied by an object, expressed in cubic units (ft³, m³, gallons, liters, etc.).
contentHTML:
What is Volume?

Volume is the measure of three-dimensional space occupied by an object or enclosed within a container, expressed in cubic units (ft³, m³, in³, cm³) or capacity units (gallons, liters). It answers: "How much space does this take up?" or "How much can this hold?"

Volume Formulas

ShapeFormulaExample
CubeV = s³4³ = 64 ft³
Rectangular PrismV = l × w × h10 × 8 × 6 = 480 ft³
CylinderV = πr²hπ × 3² × 10 = 282.7 ft³
SphereV = (4/3)πr³(4/3)π × 5³ = 523.6 ft³
ConeV = (1/3)πr²h(1/3)π × 4² × 9 = 150.8 ft³
PyramidV = (1/3) × base area × h(1/3) × 100 × 12 = 400 ft³

Volume Unit Conversions

FromToMultiply By
1 ft³gallons (US)7.481
1 ft³liters28.317
1 yd³ft³27
1 gallon (US)liters3.785
1 m³liters1,000
1 m³ft³35.314

Common Volumes

  • Bathtub: ~40–80 gallons (5.3–10.7 ft³)
  • Shipping container (20'): ~1,170 ft³
  • Olympic swimming pool: ~88,000 ft³ (660,000 gallons)
  • Concrete truck: ~8–11 cubic yards (216–297 ft³)

faq.question: How do I convert cubic feet to gallons?
faq.answer: Multiply cubic feet by 7.481 to get US gallons. Example: a 10 ft³ fish tank holds 10 × 7.481 = 74.81 gallons. Reverse: gallons ÷ 7.481 = cubic feet. For a 40-gallon water heater: 40 / 7.481 = 5.35 ft³.

faq.question: How many cubic feet in a cubic yard?
faq.answer: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet (3 × 3 × 3). This is the standard unit for ordering concrete, mulch, soil, and gravel. To convert ft³ to yd³: divide by 27. Example: a patio needing 108 ft³ of concrete = 108/27 = 4 cubic yards.

faq.question: What is the difference between volume and capacity?
faq.answer: Volume measures total 3D space (in cubic units: ft³, m³). Capacity measures how much liquid a container holds (in fluid units: gallons, liters). They measure the same thing differently: 1 ft³ = 7.481 gallons. Volume is used for solids and spaces; capacity for liquids and containers. In metric, the relationship is clean: 1 liter = 1,000 cm³ = 0.001 m³.

definition: The rate of change of an object's position with respect to time and direction — speed with a directional component, measured in m/s or ft/s.
contentHTML:
What is Velocity?

Velocity is a vector quantity that describes the rate of change of an object's position with respect to time and direction. Unlike speed (scalar — magnitude only), velocity includes both magnitude and direction.

Velocity Formulas

TypeFormulaUnits
Average Velocityv = Δx / Δt (displacement / time)m/s, ft/s, mph, km/h
Final Velocity (constant acceleration)v = v₀ + atm/s
Final Velocity (from displacement)v² = v₀² + 2aΔxm/s
Instantaneous Velocityv = dx/dt (derivative of position)m/s

Speed Comparisons

Object / EventApproximate Speed
Walking3.1 mph (1.4 m/s)
Running (average person)6–8 mph (2.7–3.6 m/s)
Usain Bolt (peak)27.8 mph (12.4 m/s)
Speed limit (highway)65–75 mph (29–34 m/s)
Commercial airplane575 mph (257 m/s)
Sound in air767 mph (343 m/s) — Mach 1
Earth's orbital speed67,000 mph (30 km/s)
Speed of light186,282 mi/s (299,792,458 m/s)

faq.question: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
faq.answer: Speed is a scalar (magnitude only): 60 mph. Velocity is a vector (magnitude + direction): 60 mph north. A car driving in a circle at constant speed has changing velocity because direction changes. Average speed = total distance / time; average velocity = displacement / time. An object returning to its start has average velocity = 0 but positive average speed.

faq.question: How do I convert between mph, km/h, and m/s?
faq.answer: 1 mph = 1.609 km/h = 0.447 m/s. 1 km/h = 0.621 mph = 0.278 m/s. 1 m/s = 2.237 mph = 3.6 km/h. Quick mental conversion: mph × 1.6 ≈ km/h (e.g., 60 mph ≈ 96 km/h). For m/s to mph: multiply by ~2.24.

faq.question: What is terminal velocity?
faq.answer: Terminal velocity is the maximum speed an object reaches when falling through a fluid (air), where the drag force equals gravitational force and acceleration becomes zero. For a human skydiver: ~120 mph (54 m/s) belly-down, ~180 mph (80 m/s) head-first. A raindrop: ~20 mph. Terminal velocity depends on mass, surface area, drag coefficient, and air density.

definition: The rate of change of velocity over time, measured in m/s² or ft/s². Positive acceleration means speeding up; negative (deceleration) means slowing down.
contentHTML:
What is Acceleration?

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time. It is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction. Positive acceleration means speeding up in the direction of motion; negative acceleration (deceleration) means slowing down.

Acceleration Formulas

FormulaUseVariables
a = Δv / ΔtAverage accelerationΔv = change in velocity, Δt = time
a = F / mNewton's Second LawF = net force, m = mass
a = (v² − v₀²) / 2ΔxFrom displacementΔx = distance traveled

Common Accelerations

SituationAcceleration
Gravity (free fall on Earth)9.81 m/s² (32.2 ft/s²) — 1g
Car accelerating (0–60 mph in 8s)~3.4 m/s² (0.34g)
Tesla Model S Plaid (0–60 in 1.99s)~13.5 m/s² (1.38g)
Fighter jet turn~60–90 m/s² (6–9g)
Space Shuttle launch~29.4 m/s² (3g)
Roller coaster max~30–60 m/s² (3–6g)
Gravity on Moon1.62 m/s² (0.17g)
Gravity on Mars3.72 m/s² (0.38g)

Kinematic Equations (Constant Acceleration)

  • v = v₀ + at
  • x = v₀t + ½at²
  • v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
  • x = ½(v₀ + v)t

faq.question: What is g-force?
faq.answer: G-force measures acceleration relative to Earth's gravitational acceleration (1g = 9.81 m/s²). It's not actually a 'force' but a measurement of acceleration felt as weight. At 2g, you feel twice your normal weight. Humans can tolerate ~5g briefly in a roller coaster, fighter pilots sustain 9g with training and g-suits, and NASA's centrifuge exceeds 20g for equipment testing. Sustained exposure above 5g causes loss of consciousness.

faq.question: Why do objects accelerate at the same rate in free fall?
faq.answer: Galileo proved (and Apollo 15 confirmed on the Moon) that all objects accelerate identically in a vacuum — 9.81 m/s² on Earth regardless of mass. A feather and a hammer dropped together in a vacuum hit at the same time. In air, drag creates differences (a feather has more air resistance relative to its weight), but the gravitational acceleration is identical for all masses.

faq.question: What is centripetal acceleration?
faq.answer: Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the center of a circular path: a = v²/r, where v is speed and r is radius. Even at constant speed, circular motion involves acceleration because the velocity direction constantly changes. A car turning at 30 mph on a 50-meter curve: a = (13.4)²/50 = 3.6 m/s² (0.37g).

definition: A push or pull on an object measured in Newtons (N). Defined by Newton's Second Law: Force = mass × acceleration (F = ma).
contentHTML:
What is Force?

Force is a push or pull that can cause an object to accelerate, decelerate, or change direction. Measured in Newtons (N) in SI units or pounds-force (lbf) in imperial. Defined by Newton's Second Law: Force = mass × acceleration.

Newton's Laws of Motion

LawStatementExample
1st (Inertia)Object at rest stays at rest; moving object stays moving unless acted on by forceSeatbelt needed — your body continues forward when car stops
2nd (F=ma)Force equals mass times accelerationHeavier objects need more force to accelerate
3rd (Action-Reaction)Every action has an equal and opposite reactionRocket pushes exhaust down, exhaust pushes rocket up

Force Conversions

UnitEquivalent
1 Newton (N)0.2248 lbf (force to hold ~100g)
1 pound-force (lbf)4.448 N
1 kilogram-force (kgf)9.807 N
1 dyne0.00001 N

Everyday Force Examples

ActionForce (approx)
Pressing a keyboard key~0.5 N
Picking up an apple~1 N
Pushing a shopping cart~20–50 N
Your weight (150 lb person)~668 N
Car engine at highway speed~500–3,000 N
Bite force (human molar)~700 N (160 lbf)

faq.question: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.answer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg — it doesn't change regardless of location. Weight is the gravitational FORCE on that mass: Weight = mass × g. A 70 kg person weighs 686 N (154 lbs) on Earth but only 114 N (26 lbs) on the Moon. Their mass is 70 kg in both places. In everyday life, we use 'weight' loosely to mean mass (pounds or kg).

faq.question: What is a Newton in everyday terms?
faq.answer: 1 Newton is roughly the force needed to hold a small apple (about 100 grams) against gravity. A 1 kg object weighs about 9.8 N. Your body weight in Newtons: multiply your weight in kg by 9.8 (or weight in lbs by 4.45). A 150-lb person experiences about 668 N of gravitational force.

faq.question: What is net force?
faq.answer: Net force is the total (vector sum) of all forces acting on an object. If you push a box with 100 N and friction opposes with 30 N, the net force is 70 N forward. If net force = 0 (balanced forces), the object is in equilibrium — either stationary or moving at constant velocity (Newton's 1st Law). Only a non-zero net force causes acceleration.

definition: The product of an object's mass and velocity (p = mv), representing the quantity of motion. Measured in kg·m/s.
contentHTML:
What is Momentum?

Momentum (p) is the product of an object's mass and velocity: p = mv. It represents the quantity of motion an object has. A heavier object or a faster object has more momentum. Momentum is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction.

Key Momentum Principles

PrincipleFormulaMeaning
Momentump = mvMass × velocity
ImpulseJ = FΔt = ΔpForce × time = change in momentum
Conservation of Momentump₁ + p₂ = p₁' + p₂'Total momentum before = after (closed system)

Momentum Comparisons

ObjectMassSpeedMomentum (kg·m/s)
Tennis ball serve0.058 kg60 m/s (134 mph)3.5
Baseball pitch0.145 kg42 m/s (95 mph)6.1
Running person75 kg3 m/s (6.7 mph)225
Car at highway speed1,500 kg30 m/s (67 mph)45,000
18-wheeler truck36,000 kg30 m/s (67 mph)1,080,000

Types of Collisions

TypeMomentumKinetic EnergyExample
ElasticConserved ✓Conserved ✓Billiard balls, atomic particles
InelasticConserved ✓Not conserved ✗Car crash, catching a ball
Perfectly InelasticConserved ✓Maximum lossObjects stick together after collision

faq.question: Why is momentum conserved?
faq.answer: Conservation of momentum is a fundamental law of physics — in a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before any interaction equals the total momentum after. This follows from Newton's 3rd Law: when two objects collide, they exert equal and opposite forces for equal time, so their momentum changes are equal and opposite, canceling out. It applies universally from atomic particles to galaxies.

faq.question: What is impulse and why do airbags work?
faq.answer: Impulse (J = FΔt) equals the change in momentum. Since the momentum change in a crash is fixed (same Δp), increasing the collision TIME reduces the FORCE. Airbags increase the deceleration time from ~0.02s (hitting steering wheel) to ~0.2s (inflating airbag), reducing the force on your body by a factor of 10. Same principle: crumple zones, helmets, and bending your knees when landing.

faq.question: How does a rocket work in space with nothing to push against?
faq.answer: Rockets work by conservation of momentum. The rocket pushes exhaust gases backward at high speed; by Newton's 3rd Law, the exhaust pushes the rocket forward. Total momentum of the system (rocket + exhaust) remains zero. The rocket doesn't push against air or the ground — it pushes against its own exhaust. This is why rockets work in the vacuum of space.

definition: The energy an object possesses due to its motion, calculated as KE = ½mv². Measured in joules (J).
contentHTML:
What is Kinetic Energy?

Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy an object possesses due to its motion. Any object that is moving has kinetic energy. The faster it moves and the more massive it is, the more kinetic energy it has.

Kinetic Energy Formula

KE = ½mv²

Where m = mass (kg) and v = velocity (m/s). Result in joules (J).

The Velocity² Factor

Because velocity is squared, doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy:

SpeedKE (relative)Stopping Distance (relative)
20 mph1×1× (~20 ft)
40 mph4×4× (~80 ft)
60 mph9×9× (~180 ft)
80 mph16×16× (~320 ft)

Types of Kinetic Energy

TypeFormulaExample
Translational½mv²Car moving on highway
Rotational½Iω²Spinning flywheel, gyroscope
ThermalAverage KE of moleculesTemperature is molecular KE

Kinetic Energy in Everyday Life

Object / EventKinetic Energy
Walking person (75 kg, 1.4 m/s)~74 J
Baseball pitch (0.145 kg, 42 m/s)~128 J
Car at 60 mph (1,500 kg, 27 m/s)~547,000 J (547 kJ)
Boeing 747 at cruise (178,000 kg, 257 m/s)~5.88 billion J (5.88 GJ)

faq.question: Why does stopping distance increase with the square of speed?
faq.answer: Kinetic energy is proportional to v², and brakes convert KE into heat. At 2× speed, you have 4× the KE to dissipate, requiring 4× the stopping distance (assuming constant braking force). This is why speed limits exist — at 80 mph, stopping distance is 16× what it is at 20 mph. This v² relationship is the single most important physics concept for driving safety.

faq.question: What is the work-energy theorem?
faq.answer: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² − ½mv₀². If you push a 10 kg box from rest to 5 m/s, you've done W = ½(10)(25) = 125 J of work. This directly connects force × distance to energy gained.

faq.question: What is the difference between kinetic and potential energy?
faq.answer: Kinetic energy is energy of MOTION (½mv²). Potential energy is STORED energy due to position or configuration (gravitational PE = mgh, elastic PE = ½kx²). They constantly convert between each other: a ball thrown upward converts KE to PE as it rises, then PE back to KE as it falls. Total mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved in the absence of friction.

definition: The stored energy an object has due to its position or configuration. Gravitational PE = mgh (mass × gravity × height).
contentHTML:
What is Potential Energy?

Potential energy (PE) is the stored energy an object has due to its position, configuration, or state. It represents the potential to do work — energy that can be converted to kinetic energy or other forms.

Types of Potential Energy

TypeFormulaExample
Gravitational PEPE = mghA book on a shelf, water behind a dam
Elastic PEPE = ½kx²Compressed spring, drawn bowstring
Chemical PEStored in molecular bondsGasoline, food, batteries
Electrical PEPE = qVCharged capacitor, lightning cloud
Nuclear PEE = mc²Nuclear reactor fuel, stellar fusion

Gravitational PE Examples

ObjectMassHeightPE (joules)
Apple on a table0.1 kg1 m0.98 J
Person on diving board75 kg10 m7,358 J
Roller coaster at peak5,000 kg50 m2,452,500 J
Water in Hoover Dam~3.5×10¹⁰ kg221 m~7.6×10¹³ J

Energy Conservation

In the absence of friction: KE + PE = constant. A roller coaster's total energy at the top (mostly PE) equals its total energy at the bottom (mostly KE). This is why the first hill must be the tallest — it sets the maximum energy for the entire ride.

faq.question: What is the difference between kinetic and potential energy?
faq.answer: Potential energy is STORED energy due to position or state. Kinetic energy is energy of MOTION. They constantly convert: a pendulum at the top has max PE and zero KE; at the bottom, max KE and zero PE. Total mechanical energy (KE + PE) stays constant without friction. Gravitational PE = mgh increases with height; KE = ½mv² increases with speed.

faq.question: Is potential energy always relative to a reference point?
faq.answer: Yes — gravitational PE depends on the chosen reference point (ground level, sea level, floor). The PE value itself changes with reference point, but the CHANGE in PE between two positions is always the same regardless of reference. This is why we only ever measure or use changes in PE, not absolute values. Convention: ground level = 0 PE for most problems.

faq.question: How is potential energy stored in food?
faq.answer: Food contains chemical potential energy stored in molecular bonds (primarily carbohydrates, fats, and proteins). When digested, these bonds are broken through metabolic processes, releasing energy. 1 food Calorie = 4,184 joules. A candy bar (~250 Cal) contains 1,046,000 J — enough energy to lift a 70 kg person ~1,525 meters (5,000 ft) straight up, theoretically.

definition: The transfer of energy when a force moves an object over a distance. Work = Force × displacement × cos(θ), measured in joules (J).
contentHTML:
What is Work in Physics?

In physics, work is done when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force. It is the transfer of energy from one system to another through the application of force over a distance, measured in joules (J).

Work Formula

W = F × d × cos(θ)

Where F = force (N), d = displacement (m), θ = angle between force and displacement.

When is Work Done?

ScenarioWork Done?Why
Pushing a box across the floorYes ✓Force causes displacement
Lifting a weight upwardYes ✓Force (upward) causes displacement (upward)
Holding a heavy box stillNo ✗No displacement — zero work (you feel tired, but physics says no work)
Carrying a box horizontallyNo ✗Force (upward support) is perpendicular to displacement (horizontal)
Wall pushing back on your handNo ✗No displacement — wall doesn't move

Work-Energy Equivalents

ActivityWork (approx)
Lifting a 1 kg book 1 meter9.8 J
Climbing one flight of stairs (75 kg person)~2,200 J
Running 1 mile~400,000 J (400 kJ)
1 kWh of electricity3,600,000 J (3.6 MJ)

faq.question: Why is holding a heavy object not 'work' in physics?
faq.answer: Work requires displacement: W = F × d. If d = 0 (no movement), W = 0 regardless of the force. When you hold a heavy box, your muscles contract isometrically (no shortening), consuming metabolic energy but doing no physics work. Your body is inefficient — muscles do internal biochemical work but the box gains no energy. This is why the physics definition of 'work' differs from everyday use.

faq.question: Can work be negative?
faq.answer: Yes! Negative work occurs when force opposes displacement. Friction does negative work on a sliding object (it slows it down, removing kinetic energy). When you lower a box slowly, gravity does positive work (force and displacement both downward) while your arms do negative work (upward force, downward displacement). Negative work means energy is being removed from the object.

faq.question: What is the relationship between work and power?
faq.answer: Power is the RATE of doing work: P = W/t (watts = joules/second). Same work done faster requires more power. Climbing a 3-meter flight of stairs does ~2,200 J of work. Walking up in 10 seconds: 220 W. Running up in 3 seconds: 733 W. The work is identical; the power is different.

definition: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, measured in watts (W). Power = Work ÷ Time.
contentHTML:
What is Power?

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, measured in watts (W). One watt equals one joule per second. Power describes HOW FAST energy is used, not how MUCH energy is used.

Power Formulas

FormulaUse
P = W / tPower = work ÷ time
P = F × vPower = force × velocity
P = ΔE / tPower = energy change ÷ time
P = V × IElectrical power = voltage × current

Power Units

UnitEquivalentContext
1 Watt (W)1 J/sSI standard
1 Kilowatt (kW)1,000 WAppliances, EV motors
1 Megawatt (MW)1,000,000 WPower plants
1 Horsepower (HP)745.7 WEngines, motors

Power in Daily Life

Device / ActivityPower
LED light bulb8–15 W
Laptop computer30–65 W
Human body (resting)~80 W
Microwave oven1,000–1,200 W
Hair dryer1,500–1,875 W
EV motor (Tesla Model 3)~211 kW peak
Commercial jet engine~80,000 kW per engine
Nuclear power plant~1,000 MW (1 GW)

faq.question: What is the difference between watts and watt-hours?
faq.answer: Watts (W) measure POWER — the rate of energy use at any instant. Watt-hours (Wh) or kilowatt-hours (kWh) measure ENERGY — the total amount used over time. A 100W bulb running for 10 hours uses 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh. Your electric bill charges for kWh (energy consumed), not watts (instantaneous power). Power is the speedometer; energy is the odometer.

faq.question: How do I calculate how much electricity something costs?
faq.answer: Cost = (watts ÷ 1,000) × hours × rate per kWh. Average US rate: ~$0.16/kWh. A 1,500W space heater running 8 hours: (1,500/1,000) × 8 × $0.16 = $1.92/day = ~$58/month. A 10W LED running 8 hours: (10/1,000) × 8 × $0.16 = $0.013/day = ~$0.40/month.

faq.question: Why is a higher-wattage appliance not always more expensive to run?
faq.answer: Because efficiency matters. A 1,500W induction cooktop might boil water in 4 minutes, while a 1,500W electric coil takes 10 minutes. Both use 1,500W, but the induction cooktop uses less total ENERGY (kWh) because it finishes faster. Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. A 10W LED bulb produces as much light as a 60W incandescent — same result, 1/6 the power.

definition: A rotational force that causes an object to rotate around an axis. Torque = Force × lever arm distance, measured in Newton-meters (N·m) or foot-pounds (ft·lb).
contentHTML:
What is Torque?

Torque (τ) is a rotational force that causes or tends to cause an object to rotate around an axis. It is the rotational equivalent of linear force and determines how effectively a force can cause angular acceleration.

Torque Formula

τ = F × r × sin(θ)

Where F = force, r = distance from axis (lever arm), θ = angle between force and lever arm. Maximum torque when θ = 90° (perpendicular).

Torque Units

UnitEquivalentContext
Newton-meter (N·m)SI standardEngineering, specifications
Foot-pound (ft·lb)1.356 N·mUS automotive, construction
Inch-pound (in·lb)0.113 N·mSmall fasteners

Torque in Automotive

Vehicle/EngineTorqueMeaning
Economy car (1.5L)110–150 ft·lbSufficient for daily driving
Midsize SUV (2.5L turbo)250–300 ft·lbGood for towing, hills
Pickup truck (5.7L V8)400–500 ft·lbHeavy towing capacity
Diesel truck600–1,000 ft·lbMaximum towing, hauling
Tesla Model 3 (electric)310 ft·lb (instant)Full torque from 0 RPM

Common Bolt Torque Specs

ApplicationTorque
Lug nuts (passenger car)80–100 ft·lb
Spark plugs12–18 ft·lb
Oil drain plug25–35 ft·lb
Head bolts60–85 ft·lb (varies by engine)

faq.question: What is the difference between torque and horsepower?
faq.answer: Torque is the rotational FORCE (how hard you can twist). Horsepower is rotational POWER (how fast you can apply that force). HP = Torque × RPM / 5,252. High torque at low RPM = great for towing and acceleration from stop. High HP at high RPM = great for top speed. Diesel engines have high torque for towing; sport cars emphasize HP for speed. Electric motors deliver peak torque instantly at 0 RPM.

faq.question: Why do electric vehicles have instant torque?
faq.answer: Electric motors produce maximum torque at 0 RPM because electromagnetic force is generated immediately when current flows through the motor windings. Internal combustion engines need to build RPM through a torque curve (peak torque at 2,000-5,000 RPM). This instant torque gives EVs their characteristic rapid acceleration off the line — a Tesla's 0-60 mph feel is largely due to instant peak torque.

faq.question: Why is a torque wrench important?
faq.answer: Over-torquing bolts can strip threads, crack castings, or stretch bolts beyond their yield point. Under-torquing can allow bolts to loosen, causing failures. Critical applications (head bolts, lug nuts, structural connections) have specific torque specs based on bolt grade, size, and material. A calibrated torque wrench ensures you apply exactly the specified torque.

definition: The resistive force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact. Friction force = μ × Normal force, where μ is the coefficient of friction.
contentHTML:
What is Friction?

Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion or tendency of motion of two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface and opposite to the direction of motion or intended motion. Without friction, walking, driving, and gripping would be impossible.

Types of Friction

TypeDescriptionRelative Magnitude
Static FrictionPrevents motion from starting. Maximum just before sliding begins.Highest (fs_max = μs × N)
Kinetic FrictionOpposes motion of sliding surfacesLower than static (fk = μk × N)
Rolling FrictionOpposes rolling motionMuch lower (~10–100× less)
Fluid Friction (Drag)Resistance through liquids/gasesDepends on speed, shape, fluid

Coefficients of Friction (μ)

Surface Pairμs (Static)μk (Kinetic)
Rubber on dry concrete0.800.65
Rubber on wet concrete0.550.40
Rubber on ice0.150.08
Metal on metal (dry)0.600.45
Wood on wood0.500.35
Teflon on steel0.040.04
Synovial joints (human)0.010.003

faq.question: Why is it harder to start pushing something than to keep it moving?
faq.answer: Static friction (before movement starts) is greater than kinetic friction (during movement). At the microscopic level, stationary surfaces form stronger interlocking bonds than sliding surfaces. Once motion begins, surface asperities don't have time to fully interlock, reducing friction. This is why pushing a heavy box requires more initial force — once sliding, less force is needed to keep it moving.

faq.question: Does friction depend on surface area?
faq.answer: For dry solid surfaces, no — this is counterintuitive but experimentally verified. Friction force depends on μ × normal force, not contact area. A 10 kg block exerts the same friction whether laying flat (large area) or on its narrow edge (small area). The reduced area increases pressure, which proportionally increases the real contact area at the microscopic level, perfectly compensating.

faq.question: Why is ice slippery?
faq.answer: Ice is slippery because a thin layer of liquid water exists on its surface even below 0°C (called a quasi-liquid layer). This quasi-liquid layer acts as a lubricant. Pressure from standing/skating may slightly contribute to local surface melting, but the primary cause is the inherent molecular disorder at the ice surface. The coefficient of friction for rubber on ice is only 0.08–0.15, compared to 0.65–0.80 on dry concrete.

definition: Mass per unit volume of a substance (ρ = m/V), typically measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³. Water's density is 1 g/cm³ or 1,000 kg/m³.
contentHTML:
What is Density?

Density (ρ) is the mass per unit volume of a substance: ρ = m/V. It tells you how tightly matter is packed together. Density determines whether objects float or sink, helps identify materials, and is fundamental in engineering, chemistry, and earth sciences.

Densities of Common Materials

MaterialDensity (kg/m³)Density (g/cm³)Float in Water?
Air (at sea level)1.2250.001225—
Styrofoam25–2000.025–0.2Yes ✓
Wood (oak)600–9000.6–0.9Yes ✓
Ice9170.917Yes ✓
Water1,0001.000—
Concrete2,3002.3No ✗
Aluminum2,7002.7No ✗
Steel7,8007.8No ✗
Copper8,9608.96No ✗
Lead11,34011.34No ✗
Gold19,30019.3No ✗

Why Density Matters

  • Buoyancy: Objects less dense than the surrounding fluid float (ships, hot air balloons)
  • Material identification: Unknown metal? Measure density to identify it
  • Engineering: Aerospace prefers low-density materials (aluminum, carbon fiber)
  • Cooking: Oil floats on water (oil density ~0.9 g/cm³ vs water 1.0)

faq.question: Why does ice float on water?
faq.answer: Ice is less dense than liquid water (0.917 vs 1.000 g/cm³). Water is nearly unique in this — most substances are denser as solids. Water molecules form a hexagonal crystal structure when freezing, spacing out further than in liquid form. This is biologically critical: if ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, killing aquatic life. Ice floats, insulating the water below.

faq.question: How do I calculate density?
faq.answer: Density = Mass / Volume. Measure mass with a scale. For regular shapes, calculate volume geometrically. For irregular shapes, use water displacement: submerge the object and measure the volume of water displaced. Example: a rock weighs 150g and displaces 50 mL of water → density = 150g / 50cm³ = 3.0 g/cm³ (likely granite or similar).

faq.question: How do ships made of steel float?
faq.answer: While steel is ~7.8× denser than water, a ship's hull encloses a large volume of air. The AVERAGE density of the entire ship (steel + air) is less than water. A solid steel block sinks; a hollow steel hull floats because the total mass divided by total volume (including the air-filled interior) is less than 1 g/cm³. This is the principle of displacement — the ship displaces water equal to its weight.

definition: Force applied per unit area, measured in Pascals (Pa) or PSI. Pressure = Force ÷ Area. 1 atm = 101,325 Pa = 14.696 PSI.
contentHTML:
What is Pressure?

Pressure is the force applied per unit area: P = F/A. It describes how concentrated a force is. The same force over a smaller area creates higher pressure (why thumbtacks work) and over a larger area creates lower pressure (why snowshoes work).

Pressure Units

UnitEquivalentCommon Use
1 Pascal (Pa)1 N/m²SI standard
1 kilopascal (kPa)1,000 PaTire pressure in metric
1 atmosphere (atm)101,325 PaStandard atmospheric pressure
1 bar100,000 PaMeteorology, scuba
1 PSI (lb/in²)6,894.76 PaUS tire pressure, pneumatics
1 mmHg (Torr)133.32 PaBlood pressure, vacuum

Everyday Pressures

SituationPressure
Atmospheric pressure at sea level14.7 PSI (101.3 kPa, 1 atm)
Car tire (recommended)32–35 PSI (220–241 kPa)
Bicycle tire80–130 PSI (550–896 kPa)
Normal blood pressure120/80 mmHg
Scuba tank3,000 PSI (207 bar)
Pressure washer1,300–4,000 PSI
Bottom of Mariana Trench15,750 PSI (1,086 bar)

faq.question: What is atmospheric pressure and why don't we feel it?
faq.answer: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is ~14.7 PSI — that's 14.7 pounds of force on every square inch of your body (~100,000 N/m²). We don't feel it because the pressure inside our bodies equals the pressure outside, creating equilibrium. You DO feel pressure changes: ear popping during flights or driving in mountains is your body adjusting to pressure differences.

faq.question: How do I convert between PSI and kPa?
faq.answer: PSI × 6.895 = kPa. kPa ÷ 6.895 = PSI. Common tire conversions: 32 PSI = 220 kPa, 35 PSI = 241 kPa, 44 PSI = 303 kPa. For bar: PSI ÷ 14.504 = bar, or kPa ÷ 100 = bar. Most modern tire gauges show both PSI and kPa.

faq.question: Why does pressure increase with depth in water?
faq.answer: Water pressure increases because the weight of water above pushes down: P = ρgh (density × gravity × depth). Every 33 feet (10.06 m) of depth adds 1 atmosphere (14.7 PSI). At 100 feet: ~4 atm total (3 water + 1 air). Scuba divers must equalize pressure and ascend slowly to avoid decompression sickness ('the bends').

definition: The fundamental electrical law stating that voltage equals current times resistance: V = I × R. Governs all DC circuit calculations.
contentHTML:
What is Ohm's Law?

Ohm's Law states the fundamental relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in an electrical circuit: V = I × R. It is the most important equation in electrical engineering and the foundation of all circuit analysis.

The Three Forms

FindFormulaExample
Voltage (V)V = I × R2A through 10Ω → 20V
Current (I)I = V / R120V across 60Ω → 2A
Resistance (R)R = V / I12V with 0.5A → 24Ω

Power Formulas (Derived from Ohm's Law)

FormulaKnown Values
P = V × IVoltage and Current
P = I² × RCurrent and Resistance
P = V² / RVoltage and Resistance

Household Circuit Example

A US household circuit: 120V, 15A breaker

  • Maximum power: P = 120V × 15A = 1,800W
  • A 100W light bulb: draws I = 100/120 = 0.83A with resistance R = 120/0.83 = 144Ω
  • A 1,500W heater: draws I = 1,500/120 = 12.5A (83% of breaker capacity)
  • Circuit limit: Don't exceed 80% of breaker rating = 1,440W for continuous loads

faq.question: Does Ohm's Law apply to AC circuits?
faq.answer: Ohm's Law applies to AC circuits when you replace R with impedance Z: V = I × Z. Impedance includes resistance plus reactance (from capacitors and inductors). For purely resistive AC loads (heaters, incandescent bulbs), V = IR works directly with RMS values. For circuits with capacitors or inductors, you must use complex impedance and power factor considerations.

faq.question: What is the water analogy for Ohm's Law?
faq.answer: Voltage = water pressure (pushes water through), Current = water flow rate (gallons/minute), Resistance = pipe narrowness (restricts flow). Higher pressure (voltage) pushes more water (current) through a pipe. A narrower pipe (higher resistance) reduces flow for the same pressure. This analogy helps visualize why V = IR: more pressure or less restriction = more flow.

faq.question: Why does a short circuit cause fires?
faq.answer: A short circuit creates a near-zero resistance path. By I = V/R, as R approaches 0, current approaches infinity. At 120V with 0.01Ω short: I = 12,000A — hundreds of times the wire's safe capacity. Power dissipated = I²R heats wires rapidly to ignition temperature. Circuit breakers and fuses exist to interrupt this current before wires overheat and cause fires.

definition: The distance between successive crests (or troughs) of a wave, measured in meters. Related to frequency by: λ = c / f.
contentHTML:
What is Wavelength?

Wavelength (λ) is the distance between successive crests, troughs, or identical points of a wave. It is measured in meters (or nanometers for light). Wavelength is inversely related to frequency: λ = c/f (or v/f for non-electromagnetic waves).

The Electromagnetic Spectrum
