Microwaves1 mm – 1 m300 MHz – 300 GHzMicrowave ovens, 5G, radar
Infrared700 nm – 1 mm300 GHz – 430 THzRemote controls, thermal imaging
Visible light380–700 nm430–790 THzHuman vision
Ultraviolet10–380 nm790 THz – 30 PHzSunburn, sterilization
X-rays0.01–10 nm30 PHz – 30 EHzMedical imaging
Gamma rays< 0.01 nm> 30 EHzCancer treatment, nuclear

Visible Light Wavelengths

ColorWavelength (nm)
Red620–750
Orange590–620
Yellow570–590
Green495–570
Blue450–495
Violet380–450

faq.question: What is the relationship between wavelength, frequency, and speed?
faq.answer: The wave equation: speed = wavelength × frequency (c = λf). For electromagnetic waves in vacuum, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s (speed of light). Longer wavelength = lower frequency (radio waves). Shorter wavelength = higher frequency (X-rays, gamma rays). For sound in air: speed ≈ 343 m/s, so a 440 Hz note (A4) has wavelength ≈ 0.78 m.

faq.question: Why is the sky blue?
faq.answer: Rayleigh scattering: shorter wavelengths (blue, ~450 nm) scatter much more than longer wavelengths (red, ~700 nm) when hitting atmospheric molecules. Blue light scatters ~5.5× more than red. So blue light reaches your eyes from all directions (scattered sky), while red/orange light passes through more directly — which is why sunsets look red (long path through atmosphere scatters away all blue).

faq.question: What wavelength is WiFi?
faq.answer: WiFi operates at two main frequency bands: 2.4 GHz (λ ≈ 12.5 cm) and 5 GHz (λ ≈ 6 cm). WiFi 6E adds 6 GHz (λ ≈ 5 cm). The 2.4 GHz band penetrates walls better (longer wavelength) but is slower. The 5 GHz band is faster but doesn't penetrate walls as well. This wavelength-penetration tradeoff is why you might have weak 5 GHz signal in far rooms.

definition: The number of complete wave cycles per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.
contentHTML:
What is Frequency?

Frequency is the number of complete cycles of a periodic event per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second. Frequency applies to sound waves, electromagnetic radiation, electrical signals, mechanical vibrations, and any repeating phenomenon.

Frequency Units

UnitValueExample
1 Hz1 cycle/secondHeartbeat at rest
1 kHz1,000 HzAudio tones
1 MHz1,000,000 HzAM radio stations
1 GHz10⁹ HzComputer processors, WiFi
1 THz10¹² HzInfrared light, security scanners

Frequency Examples

Sound/SignalFrequency
Human hearing range20 Hz – 20,000 Hz
Bass notes20–250 Hz
Middle C (piano)261.6 Hz
Concert A (tuning standard)440 Hz
Human speech range85–8,000 Hz
Dog hearing (upper limit)~65,000 Hz
US power grid60 Hz
European power grid50 Hz
WiFi (2.4 GHz band)2,400,000,000 Hz
5G (mmWave)24–100 GHz

faq.question: What is the difference between 50 Hz and 60 Hz power?
faq.answer: US/Canada/parts of South America use 60 Hz AC power; most of Europe, Asia, and Africa use 50 Hz. The frequency refers to how many times per second the AC current alternates direction. 60 Hz motors spin slightly faster. Most modern electronics (phones, laptops) handle both automatically (their power adapters say '50-60 Hz'). However, some clocks and older motors designed for one frequency may run incorrectly on the other.

faq.question: Why can't humans hear above 20,000 Hz?
faq.answer: The human cochlea (inner ear) has hair cells that respond to different frequencies. The ones for high frequencies are at the entrance and suffer the most damage from noise exposure over time. Most adults actually can't hear above 15,000-17,000 Hz. Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) primarily affects high frequencies first. Children can hear up to ~20 kHz; by age 50, many can't hear above 12 kHz.

faq.question: What is the frequency of visible light?
faq.answer: Visible light ranges from ~430 THz (red, 700 nm) to ~790 THz (violet, 380 nm) — that's 430–790 TRILLION cycles per second. These are electromagnetic waves, not sound. Related by c = λf: red light at 700 nm has f = (3×10⁸)/(700×10⁻⁹) = 4.3×10¹⁴ Hz = 430 THz.

definition: The SI unit for the amount of a substance, equal to 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) — known as Avogadro's number.
contentHTML:
What is a Mole?

The mole (mol) is the SI unit for the amount of a substance, defined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions, or other entities). This number is known as Avogadro's number. The mole bridges the gap between the atomic scale and the human scale — allowing chemists to count atoms by weighing them.

Why Moles Matter

Without MolesWith Moles
"Mix 1.204×10²⁴ molecules of H₂ with 6.022×10²³ molecules of O₂""Mix 2 mol H₂ with 1 mol O₂"
Individual atoms are ~10⁻²⁶ kg1 mol of atoms weighs the molar mass in grams

Molar Mass Reference

SubstanceMolar Mass (g/mol)Meaning
Hydrogen (H₂)2.0161 mol H₂ weighs 2.016 g
Carbon (C)12.0111 mol C weighs 12.011 g
Water (H₂O)18.0151 mol H₂O = 18 mL ≈ 1 tbsp
Sodium chloride (NaCl)58.441 mol NaCl ≈ 2 tbsp table salt
Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)180.161 mol glucose ≈ ¾ cup sugar

faq.question: How big is Avogadro's number?
faq.answer: 6.022 × 10²³ is incomprehensibly large. If you had a mole of pennies, they would cover the Earth 300 meters deep. A mole of marshmallows would blanket the US 660 miles deep. A mole of seconds = 1.9 × 10¹⁶ years — over a million times the age of the universe. Yet this many water molecules is just 18 mL (about 1 tablespoon).

faq.question: How do I convert between moles and grams?
faq.answer: Moles = grams ÷ molar mass. Grams = moles × molar mass. Example: How many moles in 36 g of water? Molar mass of H₂O = 18.015 g/mol. Moles = 36 / 18.015 = 2.0 mol. Reverse: How many grams in 0.5 mol NaCl? Grams = 0.5 × 58.44 = 29.22 g.

faq.question: Why is the mole based on carbon-12?
faq.answer: The mole was originally defined so that exactly 12 grams of carbon-12 contained one mole of atoms. This made the numerical value of molar mass (in g/mol) equal to the atomic mass (in amu) — a convenient correspondence. Since 2019, the mole is redefined by fixing Avogadro's number at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³, but the carbon-12 connection remains nearly exact.

definition: The mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol). Equal to the atomic/molecular weight read from the periodic table.
contentHTML:
What is Molar Mass?

Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol). For elements, it equals the atomic weight on the periodic table. For compounds, add the molar masses of all atoms in the formula.

How to Calculate Molar Mass

Example: Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄)

ElementAtomic MassCountSubtotal
H1.00822.016
S32.06132.06
O16.00464.00
Total Molar Mass98.08 g/mol

Common Molar Masses

SubstanceFormulaMolar Mass (g/mol)
WaterH₂O18.015
Carbon dioxideCO₂44.01
Sodium chlorideNaCl58.44
GlucoseC₆H₁₂O₆180.16
EthanolC₂H₅OH46.07
AspirinC₉H₈O₄180.16
CaffeineC₈H₁₀N₄O₂194.19

faq.question: What is the difference between molar mass and molecular weight?
faq.answer: They are numerically the same but technically different. Molar mass is the mass per mole of substance in g/mol. Molecular weight (relative molecular mass) is a dimensionless ratio compared to 1/12 of carbon-12 mass. In practice, they have the same numerical value: water = 18.015 g/mol (molar mass) = 18.015 amu (molecular weight). Use molar mass for calculations involving grams and moles.

faq.question: How do I find the molar mass of a compound?
faq.answer: Step 1: Write the chemical formula (e.g., Ca(OH)₂). Step 2: Count each atom (Ca:1, O:2, H:2). Step 3: Multiply each count by its atomic mass from the periodic table. Step 4: Sum all values. Ca(OH)₂ = 40.08 + 2(16.00) + 2(1.008) = 74.10 g/mol.

faq.question: Why is molar mass important?
faq.answer: Molar mass converts between mass (what you can weigh on a scale) and moles (what reactions require). Without it, you can't do stoichiometry. If a reaction needs 2 mol NaOH, you calculate: 2 × 40.00 = 80.00 g of NaOH to weigh out. It's the bridge between lab work (grams) and chemical equations (moles).

definition: A measure of solution concentration defined as moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L or M).
contentHTML:
What is Molarity?

Molarity (M) is the most common measure of solution concentration, defined as the number of moles of solute per liter of solution: M = mol/L. A 1 M (one molar) solution contains 1 mole of solute in 1 liter of total solution.

How to Calculate Molarity

M = moles of solute / liters of solution

Preparing a Solution Example

Make 500 mL of 0.1 M NaCl solution:

StepCalculation
1. Find moles needed0.1 mol/L × 0.5 L = 0.05 mol
2. Convert to grams0.05 mol × 58.44 g/mol = 2.922 g
3. Dissolve in waterDissolve 2.922 g NaCl in water, bring total volume to 500 mL

Common Solution Concentrations

SolutionApproximate Molarity
Seawater NaCl~0.6 M
Saline IV solution0.154 M (0.9% NaCl)
Household bleach (NaClO)~0.8 M (5.25%)
Hydrochloric acid (conc.)~12 M
Sulfuric acid (conc.)~18 M
Blood glucose (normal)~0.005 M (5 mM)

faq.question: What is the difference between molarity and molality?
faq.answer: Molarity (M) = moles of solute per liter of SOLUTION. Molality (m) = moles of solute per kilogram of SOLVENT. Molality doesn't change with temperature (mass doesn't expand), while molarity does (volume changes with temperature). Molality is preferred for precise physical chemistry work (boiling point elevation, freezing point depression). For general chemistry lab work, molarity is more practical.

faq.question: How do I dilute a solution?
faq.answer: Use the dilution equation: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂. Example: dilute 2M HCl to make 500 mL of 0.5M HCl. C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ → 2M × V₁ = 0.5M × 500mL → V₁ = 125 mL. Take 125 mL of 2M HCl and add water to reach 500 mL total volume. SAFETY: always add acid to water, never water to acid.

faq.question: What does 1M mean in practical terms?
faq.answer: 1M means 1 mole of solute dissolved in enough solvent to make 1 liter total. For NaCl (58.44 g/mol): 1M = 58.44 g in 1L — about 2 tablespoons of salt in a quart. For table sugar (342 g/mol): 1M = 342 g in 1L — about 1.5 cups of sugar in a quart. The actual mass depends on the molar mass of the substance.

definition: A measure of solution concentration defined as moles of solute per kilogram of solvent (mol/kg or m).
contentHTML:
What is Molality?

Molality (m) is a measure of solution concentration defined as the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent: m = mol solute / kg solvent. Unlike molarity, molality does not change with temperature because mass (unlike volume) is independent of temperature.

Molality vs Molarity

PropertyMolarity (M)Molality (m)
Definitionmol solute / L solutionmol solute / kg solvent
Unitsmol/L (M)mol/kg (m)
DenominatorTotal solution volumeSolvent mass only
Temperature dependent?Yes (volume changes)No (mass doesn't change)
Easier to prepare?YesSlightly harder (must weigh solvent)

Colligative Properties (Where Molality Matters)

PropertyFormulaConstant for Water
Boiling point elevationΔTb = Kb × m × iKb = 0.512 °C/m
Freezing point depressionΔTf = Kf × m × iKf = 1.86 °C/m

Example: Road salt (NaCl) at 1m concentration depresses water's freezing point by 1.86 × 1 × 2 = 3.72°C (6.7°F) because NaCl dissociates into 2 ions (i=2).

faq.question: When should I use molality instead of molarity?
faq.answer: Use molality for colligative property calculations (boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, osmotic pressure) and when temperature varies significantly during an experiment. Molality is temperature-independent because it's based on mass, not volume. For routine lab work and solution preparation, molarity is more convenient and widely used.

faq.question: How does road salt lower the freezing point?
faq.answer: Road salt (NaCl) lowers water's freezing point through freezing point depression: ΔTf = Kf × m × i. NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (i=2), doubling its effect. A typical road brine (~23% NaCl by mass ≈ 4.6 m) depresses the freezing point by ~17°C (31°F), effective to about 15°F (-9°C). Below that temperature, more intense deicers like CaCl₂ (i=3) are needed.

faq.question: How do I convert between molarity and molality?
faq.answer: m = M / (ρ − M × MM/1000), where ρ = solution density (g/mL) and MM = solute molar mass (g/mol). For dilute aqueous solutions (M < 0.1), molarity ≈ molality because 1 L of water ≈ 1 kg. The difference becomes significant only in concentrated solutions or non-aqueous solvents.

definition: A logarithmic scale (0–14) measuring the acidity or basicity of a solution. pH = -log[H⁺]. pH 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic; above 7 is basic.
contentHTML:
What is pH?

The pH scale measures the acidity or basicity (alkalinity) of a solution on a scale of 0 to 14. It is defined as pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the hydrogen ion concentration in moles per liter. Each whole pH number represents a 10-fold change in acidity.

The pH Scale

pHTypeH⁺ ConcentrationExample
0Strongly acidic1 MBattery acid
1Very acidic0.1 MHydrochloric acid
2Acidic0.01 MLemon juice, vinegar
3Acidic0.001 MOrange juice, soda
4Mildly acidic10⁻⁴ MTomato juice, acid rain
5Slightly acidic10⁻⁵ MCoffee, banana
6Slightly acidic10⁻⁶ MMilk, saliva
7Neutral10⁻⁷ MPure water
8Slightly basic10⁻⁸ MSeawater, eggs
9Basic10⁻⁹ MBaking soda
10Basic10⁻¹⁰ MMilk of magnesia
11Very basic10⁻¹¹ MAmmonia
12Very basic10⁻¹² MSoapy water
13Strongly basic10⁻¹³ MBleach, oven cleaner
14Very strongly basic10⁻¹⁴ MDrain cleaner (NaOH)

faq.question: Why is the pH scale logarithmic?
faq.answer: Because hydrogen ion concentrations in real solutions vary by a factor of 10¹⁴ (from 1 M to 10⁻¹⁴ M). A linear scale covering this range would be impractical. The log scale compresses this into 0-14. Each pH unit = 10× change in [H⁺]. pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4, and 100× more acidic than pH 5. This is why small pH changes can have big biological/chemical effects.

faq.question: What is the normal pH of blood?
faq.answer: Normal arterial blood pH is 7.35–7.45 (slightly basic). Blood pH outside 6.8–7.8 is generally fatal. The body maintains this narrow range through buffer systems (primarily carbonic acid/bicarbonate). Acidosis (pH < 7.35) and alkalosis (pH > 7.45) are serious medical conditions. This incredibly tight regulation shows how critical pH is for enzyme function and cellular processes.

faq.question: Can pH go below 0 or above 14?
faq.answer: Yes! pH can be negative for very concentrated strong acids ([H⁺] > 1 M). Concentrated HCl (~12 M) has pH ≈ −1.1. Similarly, pH can exceed 14 for very concentrated strong bases. The 0-14 range only applies to dilute aqueous solutions at 25°C. In practice, values outside 0-14 are uncommon but chemically valid.

definition: The calculation of reactants and products in chemical reactions using balanced equations and molar ratios.
contentHTML:
What is Stoichiometry?

Stoichiometry is the calculation of quantities of reactants and products in chemical reactions based on balanced chemical equations. It uses molar ratios from balanced equations to predict how much of each substance is needed or produced.

Stoichiometry Steps

StepActionExample: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
1Balance the equationAlready balanced: 2:1:2
2Convert given to moles10 g H₂ ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 4.96 mol H₂
3Use molar ratio4.96 mol H₂ × (1 mol O₂ / 2 mol H₂) = 2.48 mol O₂
4Convert to desired units2.48 mol O₂ × 32.00 g/mol = 79.4 g O₂

Key Stoichiometry Concepts

  • Molar ratio: Coefficients in balanced equation give the mole ratio (2H₂:1O₂:2H₂O)
  • Limiting reagent: The reactant that runs out first, limiting the product formed
  • Excess reagent: The reactant left over after the reaction completes
  • Theoretical yield: Maximum product possible from stoichiometry
  • Actual yield: What you actually collect (always less due to losses)
  • Percent yield: (Actual / Theoretical) × 100%

faq.question: What is a limiting reagent?
faq.answer: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is completely consumed first, determining the maximum amount of product. Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. If you have 3 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂: H₂ can make 3 mol H₂O, but O₂ can make 4 mol H₂O. H₂ runs out first → H₂ is the limiting reagent, and maximum product is 3 mol H₂O with 0.5 mol O₂ left over.

faq.question: Why is percent yield always less than 100%?
faq.answer: Real reactions rarely achieve 100% theoretical yield because of: incomplete reactions (equilibrium), side reactions producing unwanted products, mechanical losses during transfer/filtration/purification, and measurement errors. A 'good' yield depends on the reaction: 90%+ is excellent for simple reactions; 50-70% is common for complex organic syntheses; pharmaceutical multi-step syntheses may have overall yields under 10%.

faq.question: How do I balance a chemical equation?
faq.answer: Rule: same number of each type of atom on both sides. Method: (1) List all elements. (2) Start with the most complex molecule. (3) Balance metals first, then non-metals, then hydrogen, and oxygen last. (4) Use the smallest whole-number coefficients. Example: Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ becomes 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ (4 Fe and 6 O on each side).

definition: The process of reducing a solution's concentration by adding more solvent. Governed by C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ (concentration × volume before = after).
contentHTML:
What is Dilution?

Dilution is the process of reducing the concentration of a solution by adding more solvent (usually water). The total amount of solute remains the same — only the concentration changes.

The Dilution Equation

C₁V₁ = C₂V₂

Where C₁ = initial concentration, V₁ = initial volume, C₂ = final concentration, V₂ = final volume.

Dilution Examples

ProblemGivenSolution
Dilute 6M HCl to make 500 mL of 1M HClC₁=6M, C₂=1M, V₂=500mLV₁ = (1×500)/6 = 83.3 mL
What concentration if 50 mL of 4M NaOH is diluted to 200 mL?C₁=4M, V₁=50mL, V₂=200mLC₂ = (4×50)/200 = 1M
Dilute bleach 1:10 for cleaning (from 5.25%)Ratio 1:10Mix 1 part bleach + 9 parts water = 0.525%

Serial Dilution

A common laboratory technique where each dilution is performed from the previous one. A 1:10 serial dilution performed 3 times gives 1:10, 1:100, and 1:1000 concentrations. Used extensively in microbiology, immunology, and analytical chemistry.

faq.question: Why must you add acid to water (never water to acid)?
faq.answer: Adding water to concentrated acid causes the water to boil on contact with the acid surface (extremely exothermic), potentially spattering concentrated acid. Adding acid to water disperses the heat through the large volume of water safely. The mnemonic: 'Do as you oughta — add acid to water' or 'AA — add acid.' This safety rule applies to strong acids like sulfuric, hydrochloric, and nitric acid.

faq.question: What is a 1:10 dilution?
faq.answer: A 1:10 dilution means 1 part sample + 9 parts diluent = 10 parts total. NOT 1 part in 10 parts diluent (that would be 1:11). Example: 1 mL of serum + 9 mL of saline = 10 mL of 1:10 dilution. The concentration becomes 1/10 of the original. A 1:100 dilution = 1 part + 99 parts = 1/100 concentration.

faq.question: Does dilution change the pH?
faq.answer: Yes, but the effect depends on the solution type. Diluting a strong acid (pH 1) tenfold raises pH by 1 (to pH 2). But you can't dilute a solution past pH 7 — approaching neutral is the limit. Buffer solutions resist pH changes upon dilution within their buffer range. In practice, a 10× dilution of a pH 3 solution gives pH 4 (for strong acids) but may give a different result for weak acids.

definition: A unit of concentration equal to 1 part in 1,000,000 parts. 1 ppm = 1 mg/L for aqueous solutions. Used for water quality, air pollution, and trace analysis.
contentHTML:
What is PPM (Parts Per Million)?

PPM stands for parts per million — a unit of concentration equal to 1 part in 1,000,000 parts. For aqueous solutions, 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg/L. PPM is used for measuring small concentrations in water quality, air pollution, food safety, and industrial processes.

PPM Scale

UnitParts PerEquivalentAnalogy
%(percent)10010,000 ppm1 cent per dollar
‰(permille)1,0001,000 ppm1 in a thousand
ppm1,000,0001 mg/L1 second in 11.6 days
ppb1,000,000,0001 μg/L1 second in 31.7 years
ppt10¹²1 ng/L1 second in 31,700 years

Common PPM Values

MeasurementTypical PPM
CO₂ in atmosphere~425 ppm (2024)
Chlorine in tap water0.2–4 ppm (EPA max: 4 ppm)
Fluoride in water0.7 ppm (recommended)
Lead in drinking water< 15 ppb (EPA action level)
CO in air (alarm threshold)35 ppm (8-hour average)
Dissolved oxygen in healthy lake6–8 ppm

faq.question: How do I convert between ppm and percent?
faq.answer: ppm ÷ 10,000 = percent. Percent × 10,000 = ppm. Examples: 5,000 ppm = 0.5%. 1% = 10,000 ppm. Household bleach at 5.25% = 52,500 ppm sodium hypochlorite. Atmospheric CO₂ at 425 ppm = 0.0425%.

faq.question: Is 1 ppm the same as 1 mg/L?
faq.answer: For dilute aqueous solutions at standard temperature, yes — 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg/L because 1 liter of water weighs approximately 1,000,000 mg (1 kg). For non-aqueous solutions, denser liquids, or gases, this equivalence doesn't hold. For gases, ppm is typically a volume ratio (ppmv) and must be converted to mass concentration using the gas's molar mass and the ideal gas law.

faq.question: What is a safe level of chlorine in drinking water?
faq.answer: The EPA allows up to 4 ppm (4 mg/L) chlorine residual in drinking water. Most utilities maintain 0.2–2 ppm for disinfection. At 4 ppm, water may taste or smell of chlorine but is considered safe. Swimming pools maintain 1–3 ppm. Activated carbon filters effectively remove chlorine if the taste is objectionable.

definition: The weighted average mass of an atom of an element, accounting for all naturally occurring isotopes. Measured in atomic mass units (amu).
contentHTML:
What is Atomic Mass?

Atomic mass is the weighted average mass of an atom of an element, accounting for all naturally occurring isotopes and their abundances. It is measured in atomic mass units (amu) or daltons (Da), where 1 amu = 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

Atomic Mass vs Mass Number

PropertyAtomic MassMass Number
DefinitionWeighted average of all isotopesProtons + neutrons for one isotope
TypeDecimal numberWhole number
Example (Cl)35.45 amuCl-35 or Cl-37
Found onPeriodic tableIsotope notation

Calculating Weighted Average

Chlorine example:

IsotopeMass (amu)AbundanceContribution
Cl-3534.96975.77%26.50
Cl-3736.96624.23%8.96
Atomic mass35.45 amu

Why Some Atomic Masses Are Near Whole Numbers

Elements with one dominant isotope have masses very close to whole numbers (e.g., fluorine 19.00, gold 196.97). Elements with multiple abundant isotopes show fractional masses (e.g., chlorine 35.45, copper 63.55).

faq.question: Why isn't the atomic mass of carbon exactly 12?
faq.answer: The element carbon has atomic mass 12.011 (not 12.000) because it's the weighted average of TWO stable isotopes: carbon-12 (98.9%, mass exactly 12 by definition) and carbon-13 (1.1%, mass 13.003). The small amount of carbon-13 pulls the average slightly above 12. If carbon had only C-12, its atomic mass would be exactly 12.000.

faq.question: What is an atomic mass unit (amu)?
faq.answer: 1 amu (or 1 dalton, Da) = 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom = 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁴ grams. It provides a convenient scale for atomic particles: proton ≈ 1.007 amu, neutron ≈ 1.009 amu, electron ≈ 0.00055 amu. The beauty: the molar mass in g/mol has the same numerical value as the atomic mass in amu (carbon: 12.011 amu ↔ 12.011 g/mol).

faq.question: How do isotopes affect atomic mass?
faq.answer: Isotopes are atoms with same protons but different neutrons. The atomic mass on the periodic table is the weighted average based on natural isotope abundances. Magnesium: Mg-24 (79%), Mg-25 (10%), Mg-26 (11%) → atomic mass = 24.305 amu. If relative abundances change (as in enriched uranium), the average mass changes — but the standard periodic table values represent Earth's natural abundances.

definition: The number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions) in one mole of a substance: 6.022 × 10²³. Named after Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro.
contentHTML:
What is Avogadro's Number?

Avogadro's number (Nₐ) is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ — the number of particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) in one mole of a substance. Named after Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro (1776–1856), it is one of the most fundamental constants in chemistry.

How Large is 6.022 × 10²³?

AnalogyScale
A mole of pennies stackedWould make a plank 4.5 × 10¹⁷ km long (47 light-years)
A mole of rice grainsWould cover all of Earth's land mass 2 meters deep
A mole of seconds= 1.91 × 10¹⁶ years (1.4 million × age of universe)
A mole of water molecules= 18 mL (just over 1 tablespoon)

How Avogadro's Number is Used

  • Moles → Particles: N = n × Nₐ (2 mol H₂O = 2 × 6.022×10²³ = 1.204×10²⁴ molecules)
  • Particles → Moles: n = N / Nₐ (3.011×10²³ atoms = 0.500 mol)
  • Mass → Particles: N = (mass / molar mass) × Nₐ (36 g H₂O = 2 mol = 1.204×10²⁴ molecules)

How Was It Determined?

Jean Perrin determined Avogadro's number experimentally in 1908 (earning the 1926 Nobel Prize) by studying Brownian motion of particles in suspension. Modern methods use X-ray crystallography of silicon single crystals for the most precise measurements.

faq.question: How was Avogadro's number determined?
faq.answer: Several methods have been used historically: (1) Jean Perrin's Brownian motion experiments (1908) — counting particles in suspension; (2) Millikan's oil drop experiment — using the electron charge; (3) X-ray crystallography — counting atoms in a known crystal volume; (4) Modern silicon sphere method — counting atoms in a near-perfect silicon-28 sphere using X-ray interferometry. The current definition (2019) fixes Nₐ at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³.

faq.question: Why is it called 'Avogadro's' number?
faq.answer: Amedeo Avogadro (1776-1856) proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles (Avogadro's hypothesis). He never actually calculated the number himself — that was done later by Loschmidt (1865), Perrin (1908), and others. The name 'Avogadro's number' was given in his honor by Jean Perrin.

faq.question: Is Avogadro's number exact?
faq.answer: Since May 20, 2019, yes — it is defined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Before 2019, it was an experimentally measured value with uncertainty. The redefinition of the SI system (including the mole) fixed Avogadro's number by definition, similar to how the speed of light was fixed at exactly 299,792,458 m/s in 1983.

definition: The equation PV = nRT relating pressure (P), volume (V), moles of gas (n), the gas constant (R), and temperature (T) for ideal gases.
contentHTML:
What is the Ideal Gas Law?

The Ideal Gas Law combines Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws into one equation: PV = nRT. It describes the behavior of an ideal gas — a theoretical gas of point particles with no intermolecular forces. Real gases approximate ideal behavior at low pressures and high temperatures.

Variables and Units

VariableMeaningSI UnitCommon Unit
PPressurePascal (Pa)atm, mmHg, kPa
VVolumem³liters (L)
nAmount (moles)molmol
RGas constant8.314 J/(mol·K)0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K)
TTemperatureKelvin (K)K (must be absolute!)

Related Gas Laws

LawRelationshipConditions
Boyle'sP₁V₁ = P₂V₂Constant T, n
Charles'sV₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂Constant P, n
Avogadro'sV₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂Constant T, P
Gay-Lussac'sP₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂Constant V, n

STP Reference

At Standard Temperature and Pressure (0°C = 273.15 K, 1 atm): 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 liters.

faq.question: What is R (the gas constant)?
faq.answer: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) in SI units, or 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) when using liters and atmospheres. Use the value that matches your units: if V is in liters and P in atm, use 0.08206. If P is in kPa and V in liters, use 8.314. The gas constant relates the energy scale to the temperature scale per mole of substance.

faq.question: Why must temperature be in Kelvin?
faq.answer: The gas laws describe proportional relationships (double T → double V). Celsius has an arbitrary zero (water's freezing point), so 20°C is NOT twice as hot as 10°C in absolute terms. Kelvin starts at absolute zero (−273.15°C, where molecular motion stops), making 600 K genuinely twice as hot as 300 K. Using Celsius would give wrong answers in PV=nRT.

faq.question: When does the ideal gas law fail?
faq.answer: At high pressures (molecules too close, intermolecular forces matter) and low temperatures (near condensation point). Real gases deviate most when: P > 10 atm, T is near the boiling point, or the gas has strong intermolecular forces (polar molecules like H₂O, NH₃). The van der Waals equation adds corrections: (P + a/V²)(V − b) = nRT, where a accounts for attraction and b for molecular volume.

definition: A measure of solution concentration equal to the number of gram equivalents of solute per liter of solution. Used primarily in acid-base and redox chemistry.
contentHTML:
What is Normality?

Normality (N) is a concentration unit defined as the number of gram equivalents of solute per liter of solution. It is related to molarity but accounts for the reactive capacity of the substance — how many H⁺ ions (acid), OH⁻ ions (base), or electrons (redox) each molecule can donate or accept.

Normality vs Molarity

N = M × n (where n = number of equivalents per mole)

SubstanceReaction Typen (equiv/mol)Relationship
HClAcid (monoprotic)11M HCl = 1N HCl
H₂SO₄Acid (diprotic)21M H₂SO₄ = 2N H₂SO₄
H₃PO₄Acid (triprotic)31M H₃PO₄ = 3N H₃PO₄
NaOHBase11M NaOH = 1N NaOH
Ca(OH)₂Base21M Ca(OH)₂ = 2N Ca(OH)₂
KMnO₄Redox (acidic)51M KMnO₄ = 5N KMnO₄

When to Use Normality

  • Acid-base titrations: At equivalence point, N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ (simplifies calculations when acids/bases have different n values)
  • Water treatment: Hardness and alkalinity are often reported in N or meq/L
  • Redox titrations: Normality accounts for electrons transferred

faq.question: Why is normality used less often today?
faq.answer: IUPAC has recommended against using normality because it is ambiguous — the number of equivalents depends on the specific reaction. H₃PO₄ is 3N in full neutralization but 1N or 2N in partial neutralization. Molarity with stoichiometric coefficients is unambiguous. However, normality remains common in analytical chemistry, water treatment, and clinical labs because N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ simplifies titration calculations.

faq.question: How do I convert normality to molarity?
faq.answer: Molarity = Normality / n (equivalents per mole). 2N H₂SO₄ = 2/2 = 1M H₂SO₄ (diprotic acid, n=2). 3N H₃PO₄ = 3/3 = 1M H₃PO₄ (triprotic, n=3). For monoprotic acids/monobasic bases (HCl, NaOH), N = M.

faq.question: What is an equivalent in chemistry?
faq.answer: An equivalent is the amount of substance that reacts with or supplies one mole of H⁺, OH⁻, or electrons. For HCl: 1 mol = 1 eq (supplies 1 mol H⁺). For H₂SO₄: 1 mol = 2 eq (supplies 2 mol H⁺). For Ca(OH)₂: 1 mol = 2 eq (supplies 2 mol OH⁻). Equivalent weight = molar mass / n.

definition: The percentage by mass of each element in a chemical compound. Calculated as (element mass in 1 mol / molar mass of compound) × 100.
contentHTML:
What is Percent Composition?

Percent composition is the percentage by mass of each element in a chemical compound. It tells you what fraction of a compound's total mass comes from each constituent element.

Formula

% Element = (Number of atoms × atomic mass of element / molar mass of compound) × 100

Example: Water (H₂O)

ElementAtomsAtomic MassSubtotal% Composition
H21.0082.016(2.016/18.015) × 100 = 11.19%
O116.0016.00(16.00/18.015) × 100 = 88.81%
Total100.00%

More Examples

CompoundFormula% C% H% O% Other
Carbon dioxideCO₂27.3%—72.7%—
GlucoseC₆H₁₂O₆40.0%6.7%53.3%—
EthanolC₂H₅OH52.1%13.1%34.7%—
Table saltNaCl———Na 39.3%, Cl 60.7%

faq.question: How is percent composition used to find empirical formulas?
faq.answer: Step 1: Assume 100 g of compound (so % becomes grams directly). Step 2: Convert grams to moles for each element. Step 3: Divide all moles by the smallest mole value. Step 4: Round to nearest whole numbers (or multiply by 2 or 3 if needed). Example: 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O → 3.33 mol C, 6.67 mol H, 3.33 mol O → ratio 1:2:1 → empirical formula CH₂O.

faq.question: What's the difference between percent composition and mass fraction?
faq.answer: They're essentially the same concept expressed differently. Percent composition is the mass fraction × 100. Mass fraction of H in H₂O = 0.1119 = 11.19%. Both tell you what portion of the compound's mass comes from each element. Mass fraction is used more in engineering; percent composition in chemistry.

faq.question: Why must percent composition add up to 100%?
faq.answer: By the law of conservation of mass, a compound contains ONLY its constituent elements — nothing else. All the mass must be accounted for. If your percentages don't add to 100% (within rounding error), either you've missed an element or made a calculation error. This is a useful check on your work.

definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound (e.g., CH₂O for glucose, whose molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆).
contentHTML:
What is an Empirical Formula?

An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. It may or may not be the same as the molecular formula. For example, glucose has empirical formula CH₂O but molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆.

Empirical vs Molecular Formula

CompoundEmpiricalMolecularMultiple
WaterH₂OH₂O1×
Hydrogen peroxideHOH₂O₂2×
GlucoseCH₂OC₆H₁₂O₆6×
Acetic acidCH₂OC₂H₄O₂2×
BenzeneCHC₆H₆6×

Finding Empirical Formula from Experimental Data

Example: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O by mass.

StepCHO
1. Grams (assume 100g)40.0 g6.7 g53.3 g
2. Convert to moles40.0/12.01 = 3.336.7/1.008 = 6.6553.3/16.00 = 3.33
3. Divide by smallest3.33/3.33 = 16.65/3.33 = 23.33/3.33 = 1
4. Empirical formulaCH₂O

faq.question: How do I find the molecular formula from the empirical formula?
faq.answer: You need the experimental molar mass (from mass spectrometry or other methods). Divide molar mass by empirical formula mass to get the multiplier. Example: empirical formula CH₂O (mass = 30 g/mol), experimental molar mass = 180 g/mol. Multiplier = 180/30 = 6. Molecular formula = (CH₂O)×6 = C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).

faq.question: Can two different compounds have the same empirical formula?
faq.answer: Yes! Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂), and formaldehyde (CH₂O) all have the same empirical formula: CH₂O. The empirical formula alone doesn't uniquely identify a compound — you also need the molar mass to determine the molecular formula. That's why empirical formulas are a starting point, not the final answer.

faq.question: What if the mole ratios aren't whole numbers?
faq.answer: If ratios have decimals like .5, multiply all by 2. If .33 or .67, multiply by 3. If .25 or .75, multiply by 4. Example: mole ratio C:H:O = 1:2:0.5 → multiply by 2 → C₂H₄O. Another: ratio 1:1.5 → multiply by 2 → 2:3. Never round 1.5 to 2 — always multiply to get whole numbers.

definition: The actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. Can be a multiple of the empirical formula (e.g., C₆H₁₂O₆ is 6× the empirical CH₂O).
contentHTML:
What is a Molecular Formula?

A molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a single molecule of a compound. It is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula and provides more specific information about the compound.

Types of Chemical Formulas

TypeExample (Glucose)What It Shows
EmpiricalCH₂OSimplest ratio only
MolecularC₆H₁₂O₆Actual atom count
StructuralDrawing with bondsHow atoms are connected
Condensed StructuralHOCH₂(CHOH)₄CHOGroups written compactly

Finding Molecular Formula

Step 1: Find empirical formula (from percent composition)

Step 2: Calculate empirical formula mass

Step 3: Divide experimental molar mass by empirical formula mass = multiplier (n)

Step 4: Molecular formula = empirical formula × n

Examples

CompoundEmpiricalEF MassActual MassnMolecular
EthyleneCH₂14282C₂H₄
BenzeneCH13786C₆H₆
SucroseC₁₂H₂₂O₁₁3423421C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁

faq.question: What is the difference between molecular and empirical formulas?
faq.answer: The empirical formula gives the simplest integer ratio of atoms. The molecular formula gives the actual count. They can be identical (H₂O is both) or differ by a whole-number multiple (benzene: empirical CH, molecular C₆H₆ = 6× the empirical). Ionic compounds (NaCl, CaCO₃) technically only have empirical formulas since they form crystal lattices, not discrete molecules.

faq.question: How do I determine the molar mass experimentally?
faq.answer: Several methods: (1) Mass spectrometry — most precise, directly measures molecular mass. (2) Freezing point depression — dissolve compound, measure ΔTf, calculate using ΔTf = Kf × m. (3) Vapor density — for gases, measure mass of known volume at known T and P, use PV=nRT. (4) Gel permeation chromatography — for polymers. Mass spectrometry is the modern standard for small molecules.

faq.question: Can a molecular formula tell you the structure?
faq.answer: No — the molecular formula alone doesn't show how atoms are connected. C₂H₆O could be ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH, a drinkable alcohol) or dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃, a gas). These are called isomers — same molecular formula, different structures, completely different properties. You need structural formulas, NMR spectroscopy, or X-ray crystallography to determine structure.

definition: The maximum distance an electric vehicle can travel on a single full battery charge, measured in miles. Affected by speed, temperature, terrain, and driving style.
contentHTML:
What is EV Range?

EV range is the maximum distance an electric vehicle can travel on a single full battery charge, measured in miles. It is the EV equivalent of a gas car's miles per tank and is the single most important specification for prospective EV buyers.

2024 EV Range Comparison

VehicleBatteryEPA RangePrice (MSRP)
Tesla Model S Long Range100 kWh405 miles~$74,990
Mercedes EQS 450+108.4 kWh350 miles~$104,400
Tesla Model 3 Long Range82 kWh358 miles~$42,490
Hyundai Ioniq 6 SE AWD77.4 kWh361 miles~$38,615
Chevrolet Equinox EV85 kWh319 miles~$33,900
Nissan Leaf S40 kWh149 miles~$28,140

Factors That Affect Range

  • Speed: Range drops ~15% at 75 mph vs 60 mph (aerodynamic drag increases with v²)
  • Temperature: Cold weather can reduce range 20–40% (battery heating + cabin heating)
  • HVAC: Air conditioning reduces range ~10–17%, heating 25–35%
  • Terrain: Mountainous driving reduces range significantly (but regenerative braking helps on descents)
  • Driving style: Aggressive acceleration can reduce range by 20–30%

faq.question: What is the difference between EPA range and real-world range?
faq.answer: EPA range is the official US government estimate based on standardized test cycles. Real-world range is typically 10–20% less, depending on driving conditions. Highway driving at 70+ mph, cold weather, and using AC/heat all reduce range below EPA estimates. Some brands (like Hyundai/Kia) tend to exceed EPA estimates in real-world tests, while others may fall short.

faq.question: How much range do I need daily?
faq.answer: The average American drives about 37 miles per day. Any EV with 200+ miles of range provides comfortable daily driving with ample buffer. For road trips, you need DC fast charging infrastructure along your route. Most EV owners charge at home overnight (Level 2) and never worry about range for daily driving.

faq.question: Does EV range degrade over time?
faq.answer: Yes, but slowly. Most EV batteries retain 80–90% of original capacity after 8–10 years and 100,000+ miles. A 300-mile EV might have 240–270 miles after 8 years. Tesla's data shows ~12% degradation at 200,000 miles. All major manufacturers warranty batteries for 8 years / 100,000 miles (minimum 70% capacity retained).

definition: Kilowatt-hours — the unit measuring an EV battery's total energy storage capacity. A larger kWh battery provides more range (e.g., 60 kWh ≈ 230 miles).
contentHTML:
What is kWh (Battery Capacity)?

Kilowatt-hours (kWh) measures an EV battery's total energy storage capacity. A larger kWh battery stores more energy and generally provides more range. It is the EV equivalent of a gas tank's gallons — the bigger the "tank," the farther you can go.

Battery Size Comparison

VehicleBattery (kWh)EPA RangeEfficiency (mi/kWh)
Nissan Leaf S40 kWh149 mi3.73
Chevrolet Bolt EV65 kWh259 mi3.98
Tesla Model 3 SR+60 kWh272 mi4.53
Tesla Model 3 LR82 kWh358 mi4.37
Ford F-150 Lightning131 kWh320 mi2.44
Hummer EV212 kWh329 mi1.55

Battery Capacity vs Range

A bigger battery doesn't always mean more range. Efficiency (mi/kWh) matters equally:

  • Tesla Model 3: 60 kWh battery, 4.5 mi/kWh → 272 miles
  • Hummer EV: 212 kWh battery, 1.55 mi/kWh → 329 miles
  • The Hummer has 3.5× the battery but only 1.2× the range (because it weighs 9,000 lbs)

faq.question: How much does it cost to charge a kWh?
faq.answer: Average US residential rate: ~$0.16/kWh. A 60 kWh battery (Tesla Model 3) costs about $9.60 for a full charge from empty. At 3.5 mi/kWh, that's ~$0.046/mile (vs ~$0.14/mile for a 30 MPG gas car at $4.20/gallon). Public DC fast charging costs more: $0.30–0.50/kWh, making a full charge $18–30.

faq.question: How long does it take to charge different battery sizes?
faq.answer: Level 1 (120V): adds ~1 kWh/hr = 3-5 miles/hour. A 60 kWh battery: 60 hours. Level 2 (240V, 32A): adds ~7-10 kWh/hr. A 60 kWh battery: 6-8 hours (overnight). DC Fast Charging: 50-350 kW, charges 10-80% in 20-40 minutes. Larger batteries take longer at the same charger power, but most DC fast chargers are 150-350 kW — handling even large batteries quickly.

faq.question: Is a bigger battery always better?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Bigger batteries add cost ($100-150/kWh at the pack level), weight (a 100 kWh pack weighs ~1,000-1,400 lbs), and charging time. For daily commuters (30-50 miles/day), a 40-60 kWh battery is ample. Larger batteries (75-100+ kWh) are best for those who regularly take road trips or live in cold climates where range drops significantly.

definition: The three tiers of EV charging speed: Level 1 (120V household, 3–5 mi/hr), Level 2 (240V, 15–30 mi/hr), Level 3 DC Fast Charging (200–1,000+ mi/hr).
contentHTML:
EV Charging Levels Explained

EV charging is categorized into three levels based on power delivery and charging speed. Understanding these levels helps you plan home charging installations, road trips, and evaluate charging infrastructure.

Charging Level Comparison

FeatureLevel 1Level 2Level 3 (DC Fast)
Voltage120V AC240V AC200-1000V DC
Power1.2-1.8 kW3.3-19.2 kW50-350+ kW
Miles added/hour3-5 mi/hr15-30 mi/hr180-1,000+ mi/hr
Full charge time (60 kWh)40-60 hours4-10 hours20-45 minutes (10-80%)
Cost per kWh$0.13-0.18 (home)$0.13-0.18 (home)$0.30-0.50 (public)
Where foundAny outletHome install, workplacesHighway corridors, commercial
Equipment cost$0 (included with EV)$300-700 + install$50,000-150,000

Charging Recommendation by Use Case

  • Daily commuter (< 40 mi/day): Level 1 may suffice (overnight = ~40 miles)
  • Average EV owner: Level 2 at home (the "gold standard") — overnight charges any EV
  • Road trippers: Level 3 at highway stops (20-40 min for 200+ miles)
  • Apartment dwellers: Workplace Level 2 or public Level 2/3

faq.question: Can I install Level 2 charging at home?
faq.answer: Yes, and most EV owners do. Requirements: a 240V outlet (like a dryer outlet, NEMA 14-50) or a hardwired EVSE. Cost: $300-700 for the charger + $200-1,000 for electrical installation (depends on panel capacity and distance). A 40A circuit provides ~30 miles of range per hour of charging — fully charging any EV overnight. Some utilities offer EV charging rate discounts.

faq.question: Will DC fast charging damage my battery?
faq.answer: Occasional DC fast charging is fine and built into the battery management system. Frequent exclusive use of DC fast charging (like daily) can accelerate battery degradation slightly — studies show ~10% more degradation over the battery's life for EV owners who primarily DC fast charge vs Level 2 home charge. This is because the high power generates more heat. For optimal battery life, use Level 2 as your primary charging method.

faq.question: What is the difference between CCS, CHAdeMO, and Tesla NACS?
faq.answer: These are connector standards: CCS (Combined Charging System) is the US/EU standard adopted by most manufacturers. CHAdeMO is Japan's standard (Nissan Leaf). Tesla's NACS (North American Charging Standard) is now adopted as the SAE J3400 standard — most manufacturers are transitioning to NACS by 2025-2026. Tesla owners can use the Supercharger network; NACS adapters let other EVs use it too.

definition: The EV equivalent of miles per gallon — how many miles an EV travels per kilowatt-hour of energy consumed. Typical range: 3–4 mi/kWh.
contentHTML:
What is Miles Per kWh?

Miles per kWh (mi/kWh) is the EV efficiency metric — how many miles an EV travels per kilowatt-hour of energy consumed. It is the direct equivalent of miles per gallon (MPG) for gas cars. Higher mi/kWh = more efficient = lower cost per mile.

EV Efficiency Rankings

Vehiclemi/kWhkWh/100 miMPGe
Hyundai Ioniq 6 SE RWD4.3523.0140
Tesla Model 3 RWD4.5322.1132
Chevrolet Bolt EV3.9825.1120
Tesla Model Y LR3.6527.4122
BMW iX xDrive502.9533.9100
Ford F-150 Lightning2.4441.078
Hummer EV Pickup1.5564.547

Cost Per Mile Comparison

Vehicle TypeEfficiencyFuel CostCost/Mile
Efficient EV (4 mi/kWh)4 mi/kWh$0.16/kWh$0.04/mi
Average EV (3 mi/kWh)3 mi/kWh$0.16/kWh$0.053/mi

Average gas car (25 MPG)25 MPG$3.50/gal$0.14/mi
Pickup truck (18 MPG)18 MPG$3.50/gal$0.194/mi

faq.question: What is a good mi/kWh rating?
faq.answer: 3.5-4.5 mi/kWh is efficient (sedans, compact SUVs). 2.5-3.5 mi/kWh is average (midsize SUVs). Below 2.5 mi/kWh is inefficient (large trucks, SUVs). The most efficient production EVs achieve 4.0-4.5+ mi/kWh. For context, 4 mi/kWh at $0.16/kWh = $0.04/mile — about 3.5× cheaper than a 30 MPG gas car at $4.20/gallon.

faq.question: Why does mi/kWh drop at highway speeds?
faq.answer: Aerodynamic drag increases with the square of speed — at 75 mph, drag is 56% higher than at 60 mph. Since EVs have no transmission losses to overcome at low speed (unlike gas cars), they are most efficient in city driving (the opposite of gas cars). Most EVs achieve their best mi/kWh at 25-35 mph and lose 15-30% of rated efficiency at 75+ mph.

faq.question: How does cold weather affect efficiency?
faq.answer: Cold weather reduces EV efficiency by 20-40%: battery heating (maintaining optimal 70°F operating temperature), cabin heating (no waste heat from an engine to use), increased rolling resistance from cold tires, and reduced battery chemistry performance. In 20°F weather, a 4 mi/kWh EV might drop to 2.4-3.2 mi/kWh. Heat pumps (standard on newer EVs) reduce this penalty by 30-50%.

definition: A system in EVs and hybrids that recovers kinetic energy during braking and converts it back to electrical energy stored in the battery, improving efficiency 10–25%.
contentHTML:
What is Regenerative Braking?

Regenerative braking is a system in EVs and hybrids that recovers kinetic energy during deceleration and converts it back to electrical energy stored in the battery. When you lift off the accelerator or brake, the electric motor runs in reverse as a generator, slowing the car while recharging the battery.

How It Works

PhaseWhat Happens
AcceleratingBattery → motor → wheels (consumes energy)
Coasting/braking (regen)Wheels → motor acts as generator → battery (recovers energy)
Hard brakingRegen + friction brakes (combined stopping power)

Energy Recovery

  • Regenerative braking recovers 10–25% of energy in typical driving
  • City driving recovers more (frequent stops) than highway (fewer stops)
  • One-pedal driving mode maximizes regen by using strong deceleration when lifting off the accelerator
  • Regen is limited when the battery is at 100% (no room to store recovered energy)

Regen Benefits

BenefitImpact
Extended range10-25% more miles, especially in city driving
Brake pad longevityBrake pads last 2-3× longer (100K+ miles in some EVs)
Reduced brake dustLess particulate matter pollution from brake wear
One-pedal drivingMore comfortable driving experience once adapted

faq.question: What is one-pedal driving?
faq.answer: One-pedal driving is a mode where regenerative braking is strong enough that lifting your foot off the accelerator decelerates the car to a complete stop — you rarely need the brake pedal. Most EVs offer adjustable regen levels. Advocates love it for smooth, intuitive driving in traffic. It takes 1-2 days to adapt but most EV drivers prefer it once accustomed. Brake lights activate automatically during strong regen.

faq.question: Does regenerative braking completely replace friction brakes?
faq.answer: No — friction brakes are still needed for emergency stops, very steep descents, and situations where regen alone can't provide enough braking force. Regen is also limited at very low speeds (below ~5 mph) and when the battery is fully charged. However, in daily driving with one-pedal mode, you might use friction brakes only 10-20% as often, dramatically extending brake pad life.

faq.question: Why is regen less effective in cold weather?
faq.answer: Cold batteries have higher internal resistance, limiting how fast they can accept charge. This means the motor can't regenerate as much energy during braking in cold weather, reducing regen effectiveness by 30-50%. The car compensates by using more friction braking. As the battery warms up during driving, regen effectiveness improves. Pre-conditioning the battery (many EVs do this automatically before DC fast charging) also helps.

definition: The gradual loss of an EV battery's maximum capacity over time and charge cycles. Most EV batteries retain 80–90% capacity after 8–10 years.
contentHTML:
What is Battery Degradation?

Battery degradation is the gradual, irreversible loss of an EV battery's maximum capacity over time and charge cycles. All lithium-ion batteries degrade, but modern EV batteries are designed to last well beyond a decade with proper care.

Typical Degradation Timeline

Age/MileageTypical Capacity RemainingRange Example (originally 300 mi)
New100%300 miles
2 years / 30K mi95-98%285-294 miles
5 years / 75K mi90-95%270-285 miles
8 years / 100K mi85-92%255-276 miles
10 years / 150K mi80-90%240-270 miles
15 years / 200K mi75-85%225-255 miles

Factors That Accelerate Degradation

FactorImpactRecommendation
Frequent DC fast chargingHighUse Level 2 as primary charging
Charging to 100% dailyModerateCharge to 80% for daily use
Extreme heat exposureHighPark in shade, use battery cooling
Letting battery sit at 0% or 100%ModerateKeep 20-80% for storage
Aggressive drivingLow-moderateModerate acceleration when possible

faq.question: How long do EV batteries last?
faq.answer: Most EV batteries are expected to last 15-20 years or 300,000+ miles. All major manufacturers warranty the battery for 8 years/100,000 miles with 70% minimum capacity. Real-world data shows Tesla batteries retaining ~88% after 200,000 miles. Battery technology is improving — newer chemistries (LFP, solid-state) promise even better longevity.

faq.question: Should I charge to 100% every day?
faq.answer: No — for daily driving, charging to 80% is recommended for lithium-ion batteries (NCA/NMC chemistry). Keeping the battery between 20-80% reduces stress on the cells and slows degradation. Charge to 100% only before long trips when you need full range. LFP batteries (Tesla Standard Range, some BYD models) are more tolerant of 100% charging.

faq.question: How much does a battery replacement cost?
faq.answer: A full battery replacement costs $5,000-$15,000+ depending on the vehicle and battery size (before labor). Individual module replacement can be $1,000-3,000. However, complete replacement is rare — most batteries outlast the vehicle. Battery costs are dropping (~$100/kWh in 2024, down from $1,200/kWh in 2010). Third-party remanufactured batteries are an emerging lower-cost option.

definition: Level 3 EV charging that delivers high-voltage DC power directly to the battery, bypassing the onboard charger. Can charge 10–80% in 20–40 minutes.
contentHTML:
What is DC Fast Charging?

DC Fast Charging (DCFC), also called Level 3 charging, delivers high-voltage direct current (DC) power directly to the EV battery, bypassing the vehicle's onboard AC-to-DC converter. This enables dramatically faster charging compared to Level 1 or Level 2.

DC Fast Charging Speeds

ChargerMax Power10-80% Time (75 kWh battery)
50 kW (CHAdeMO/older CCS)50 kW~60-75 min
150 kW (CCS)150 kW~25-35 min
250 kW (Tesla Supercharger V3)250 kW~15-25 min
350 kW (CCS Hyper-fast)350 kW~12-18 min

The Charging Curve

EVs don't charge at constant speed. The rate slows as the battery fills to protect battery health:

  • 10-50%: Near-maximum charging speed (peak kW)
  • 50-80%: Speed tapers gradually (still fast)
  • 80-100%: Speed drops significantly (may take as long as 10-80%)

This is why charging recommendations say "charge to 80%" at DCFC — the last 20% is slow and expensive.

faq.question: Why does charging slow down after 80%?
faq.answer: The Battery Management System (BMS) reduces charging power to protect the battery's longevity and safety. As cells approach full charge, the internal resistance increases and the voltage difference shrinks, requiring careful trickle charging. Pushing high power into a nearly-full battery causes excessive heat and accelerated degradation. The 10-80% window is the 'sweet spot' for fast charging.

faq.question: How much does DC fast charging cost?
faq.answer: DC fast charging typically costs $0.30-0.50/kWh — about 2-3× the cost of home charging. A 60 kWh charge at $0.40/kWh = $24 (vs ~$9.60 at home). Some networks charge per minute instead, which penalizes vehicles with slower peak charging rates. Tesla Supercharging averages $0.25-0.35/kWh for Tesla owners.

faq.question: Can all EVs use DC fast charging?
faq.answer: Almost all modern EVs support DC fast charging, but the maximum charging speed varies widely. The Nissan Leaf limited to 50 kW CHAdeMO. The Tesla Model 3 accepts up to 250 kW. The Hyundai Ioniq 5 handles up to 350 kW (with 800V architecture). The actual charging speed is limited by the SLOWER of: the charger's maximum output or the vehicle's maximum acceptance rate.

definition: The current battery level expressed as a percentage of total capacity (0–100%), analogous to a fuel gauge in conventional vehicles.
contentHTML:
What is State of Charge?

State of Charge (SOC) is the current charge level of an EV battery expressed as a percentage (0–100%), analogous to a fuel gauge in conventional vehicles. The SOC tells you how much usable energy remains in the battery.

SOC Operating Windows

SOC RangeUsageBattery Health Impact
0-10%Emergency only — find a chargerStress on cells; avoid regularly
10-20%Low — plan charging soonAcceptable if not sustained
20-80%Optimal daily rangeBest for battery longevity ✓
80-90%Fine for daily drivingMinimal impact
90-100%Before long tripsAvoid keeping at 100% for extended periods

SOC vs Usable Capacity

The SOC displayed to you is the usable SOC. EVs maintain a hidden buffer: the battery never truly reaches 0% or 100% at the cell level. Typically, 5-10% of total capacity is held in reserve — "0%" still has some charge to protect the battery from deep discharge, and "100%" isn't the true maximum to prevent overcharging.

faq.question: What happens if SOC reaches 0%?
faq.answer: The car enters 'limp mode' or 'turtle mode' before reaching displayed 0% — reducing speed and power to conserve remaining energy. At displayed 0%, the car can usually still roll at low speed for 1-5 miles (from the hidden buffer). After that, the car stops completely but the 12V system stays on briefly. Towing or a mobile charging service is needed. Running the battery to 0% is stressful for the cells but won't permanently damage a modern EV battery in a single occurrence.

faq.question: Should I charge to 100% for road trips?
faq.answer: Yes — before a road trip, charging to 100% is fine and recommended. The concern is keeping the battery at 100% for extended periods (days/weeks), not briefly reaching 100%. Set your charge limit to 80% for daily use, then bump to 100% the night before a trip. LFP batteries (some Teslas, Chinese EVs) can be charged to 100% regularly without significant degradation.

faq.question: What is Depth of Discharge (DOD)?
faq.answer: Depth of Discharge = 100% − SOC. If you charge to 80% and drive down to 20%, your DOD is 60% (a 60% 'cycle'). Shallow cycles (small DOD) put less stress on the battery than deep cycles. A battery that repeatedly cycles 20-80% (60% DOD) will last significantly longer than one cycled 0-100% (100% DOD). This is the basis of the '20-80% rule' for daily charging.

definition: A federal tax incentive of up to $7,500 for qualifying new electric vehicles under the Inflation Reduction Act, subject to MSRP caps and income limits.
contentHTML:
What is the EV Tax Credit?

The EV federal tax credit is a tax incentive of up to $7,500 for qualifying new electric vehicles under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022. Starting January 2024, the credit can be applied as a point-of-sale discount at the dealership instead of waiting until tax filing.

2024 Eligibility Requirements

RequirementNew EVsUsed EVs
Maximum credit$7,500$4,000
MSRP cap — Sedans$55,000$25,000
MSRP cap — SUVs/Trucks/Vans$80,000$25,000
Single filer income limit$150,000 AGI$75,000 AGI
Married filing jointly$300,000 AGI$150,000 AGI
Final assemblyNorth America requiredAny
Battery sourcingComponent + mineral requirementsNo requirement

Credit Breakdown (New EVs)

  • $3,750 for meeting battery component requirements (% assembled in North America)
  • $3,750 for meeting critical mineral requirements (% sourced from US/free trade partners)
  • Total: up to $7,500 if both criteria are met

faq.question: Which EVs qualify for the full $7,500 credit in 2024?
faq.answer: The list changes as manufacturers adjust sourcing. As of early 2024, qualifying models include: Tesla Model 3, Model Y (some trims); Chevrolet Bolt, Equinox EV, Blazer EV; Ford Mustang Mach-E, F-150 Lightning; Chrysler Pacifica PHEV; and several others. Check fueleconomy.gov for the current list — it is updated as manufacturers certify compliance with battery sourcing requirements.

faq.question: Can I get the credit at the dealership?
faq.answer: Starting January 1, 2024, yes — dealers can apply the credit as a point-of-sale price reduction, so you get the discount immediately instead of waiting until you file taxes. The dealer must register with the IRS and the vehicle must qualify. Not all dealers are set up for this, so confirm before purchase. You still need to meet income requirements.

faq.question: Do state EV incentives stack with the federal credit?
faq.answer: Yes! Many states offer additional incentives: California ($2,000-$7,500 rebate), Colorado ($5,000 credit), New York ($2,000 rebate), and others. These stack with the federal $7,500 credit for potential savings of $10,000-$15,000+. Some utilities also offer EV charging discounts or rebates on home charger installation. Check dsireusa.org for state-specific incentives.

definition: The complete cost of owning a vehicle over its lifetime, including purchase price, fuel/electricity, insurance, maintenance, depreciation, and tax incentives.
contentHTML:
What is Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)?

Total Cost of Ownership is the complete cost of owning a vehicle over its lifetime, including purchase price, fuel/electricity, insurance, maintenance, depreciation, and tax incentives. TCO is the most accurate way to compare the true cost of an EV versus a gas car.

TCO Comparison: EV vs Gas Car (5-Year)

Cost CategoryGas Car (avg sedan)EV (avg sedan)EV Savings
Purchase price$32,000$35,000-$3,000
Federal tax credit$0-$7,500+$7,500
Fuel (60K mi over 5yr)$8,400 (30 MPG, $4.20/gal)$2,880 (3.5 mi/kWh, $0.168/kWh)+$5,520
Maintenance$4,500$1,800+$2,700
Insurance$7,500$8,250-$750
Depreciation$16,000 (50%)$14,000 (40%)+$2,000
5-Year TCO$68,400$54,430+$13,970

Why EV Maintenance Costs Less

  • No oil changes ($75/each, 3-4× per year)
  • No transmission fluid service
  • Brake pads last 2-3× longer (regenerative braking)
  • No spark plugs, timing belts, or exhaust system
  • Fewer moving parts (~20 in motor vs ~2,000 in engine)

faq.question: Are EVs cheaper to own than gas cars?
faq.answer: In most cases, yes. While EVs often have higher upfront costs, lower fuel costs (~$0.04/mile vs $0.12+/mile), lower maintenance (~60% less), and federal tax credits ($7,500) make them cheaper over 5-10 years. The breakeven point is typically 2-3 years. Exceptions: if you drive very few miles, if electricity is expensive in your area (>$0.30/kWh), or if you buy an EV that doesn't qualify for tax credits.

faq.question: How much do you save on maintenance with an EV?
faq.answer: EVs save approximately 40-60% on maintenance compared to gas cars. Over 100,000 miles: EV maintenance costs ~$4,600 vs $9,200 for gas (AAA estimates). No oil changes, no transmission service, brake pads last 100K+ miles (regen braking), no exhaust system repairs. Main EV maintenance: tire rotation, cabin air filter, wiper fluid, and eventual brake fluid change.

faq.question: Do EVs hold their value?
faq.answer: Early EVs depreciated heavily, but modern EVs hold value well — similar to or better than gas equivalents. Teslas consistently rank among the lowest-depreciation vehicles (40% after 5 years vs 60% for average cars). As range anxiety decreases and charging infrastructure grows, EV resale values are strengthening. Battery health is the key factor — EVs with well-maintained batteries retain more value.

definition: Miles Per Gallon equivalent — the EPA metric comparing EV energy consumption to gasoline. 33.7 kWh of electricity = 1 gallon of gas energy content.
contentHTML:
What is MPGe?

MPGe (Miles Per Gallon equivalent) is the EPA metric for comparing the fuel efficiency of electric vehicles to gasoline vehicles. It is based on the energy equivalence: 33.7 kWh of electricity = 1 gallon of gasoline (in terms of energy content).

How MPGe is Calculated

MPGe = 33.7 / (kWh per mile)

Or equivalently: MPGe = 33.7 × mi/kWh

MPGe Comparison

VehicleMPGemi/kWhClass
Hyundai Ioniq 6 SE RWD1404.15Sedan
Tesla Model 3 RWD1323.92Sedan
Chevrolet Bolt EV1203.56Hatchback
Kia EV6 RWD1173.47Crossover
BMW iX xDrive501002.97Luxury SUV
Ford F-150 Lightning782.31Pickup truck
Best gas car: Toyota Prius57 MPG—Hybrid sedan

Even the least efficient EV (Hummer EV at 47 MPGe) approaches the most efficient gas car (Prius at 57 MPG), showing how much more efficient electric drivetrains are at converting fuel to motion.

faq.question: Is MPGe a fair comparison to MPG?
faq.answer: MPGe compares energy content equally (33.7 kWh ≈ 1 gallon of gas energy), but critics argue it doesn't account for power generation losses. Electricity generation is ~33-60% efficient depending on the source, while the gas tank is 100% 'efficient' energy delivery (combustion losses happen in the engine). However, even accounting for grid generation losses, EVs are ~2-3× more efficient 'well-to-wheel' than gas cars.

faq.question: Why are EVs so much more efficient than gas cars?
faq.answer: Electric motors convert ~85-95% of electrical energy to wheel motion. Gas engines convert only ~20-35% of fuel energy to motion — the rest becomes waste heat. This fundamental efficiency difference means EVs need 2-4× less energy to travel the same distance. It's also why EVs don't need cooling systems as large as gas cars and why regenerative braking (recovering energy during deceleration) is possible.

faq.question: What does 33.7 kWh = 1 gallon mean?
faq.answer: One gallon of gasoline contains 33.7 kWh of chemical energy (121 MJ or 115,000 BTU). This is the basis for MPGe: if an EV uses 33.7 kWh to travel X miles, it achieves X MPGe. However, a gas car using 1 gallon converts only ~7 kWh to motion (the rest is heat). An EV using 33.7 kWh delivers ~30 kWh to the wheels. This is why 100 MPGe >> 100 MPG in real-world cost savings.

definition: Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment — the infrastructure that delivers electricity to charge an EV. Includes home chargers, workplace chargers, and public charging networks.
contentHTML:
What is EVSE?

EVSE (Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment) is the complete system that delivers electricity from the grid to an EV's battery. While commonly called a "charger," the actual charging circuitry is onboard the vehicle — the EVSE is the connection and safety equipment between the building's electrical system and the car.

Types of EVSE

TypeLevelPowerCost
Portable L1 EVSE (included with EV)Level 11.2-1.8 kW$0 (included)
Home wall-mount L2 EVSELevel 27.2-11.5 kW$300-700
Commercial L2 EVSELevel 27.2-19.2 kW$1,500-5,000
DC Fast Charging stationLevel 350-350+ kW$50,000-150,000+

Major US Charging Networks

NetworkStationsConnectorPricing
Tesla Supercharger~2,000+ locationsNACS (opening to CCS)$0.25-0.35/kWh
ChargePoint~40,000+ Level 2J1772, CCSVaries (host-set)
Electrify America~800+ DC fastCCS$0.31-0.43/kWh
