faq.question: What home EVSE should I buy?
faq.answer: For most homes: a 240V, 40A Level 2 EVSE (delivers ~9.6 kW / 30 mi of range per hour). Top-rated options: ChargePoint Home Flex ($500-600, adjustable amperage), Grizzl-E ($400, weatherproof), Tesla Wall Connector ($475, best for Tesla owners). Choose hardwired for permanent install or NEMA 14-50 plug for portability. WiFi connectivity is useful for scheduling charging during off-peak electricity hours.

faq.question: How much does EVSE installation cost?
faq.answer: The EVSE unit itself: $300-700 for a home Level 2. Electrical installation: $200-2,000 depending on your panel's capacity, distance from panel to garage, and local codes. Total: typically $500-2,500. If your electrical panel needs an upgrade (200A service), add $1,500-4,000. Many utilities and states offer rebates ($200-500) for home EVSE installation.

faq.question: Can I use a regular outlet to charge my EV?
faq.answer: Yes — every EV comes with a portable Level 1 EVSE that plugs into a standard 120V household outlet (NEMA 5-15). It adds 3-5 miles of range per hour, which means ~40-50 miles overnight. For a 40-mile daily commute, Level 1 is sufficient. For longer needs, Level 2 (240V) is recommended. Never use an extension cord — use a dedicated circuit with the EVSE plugged directly into the outlet.

definition: A profitability metric measuring the percentage return on an investment relative to its cost: ROI = (Net Profit / Cost of Investment) × 100.
contentHTML:
What is ROI (Return on Investment)?

Return on Investment (ROI) measures the gain or loss from an investment relative to its cost, expressed as a percentage. It is the most widely used metric for evaluating the efficiency of an investment.

ROI Formula

ROI = ((Gain − Cost) / Cost) × 100

ROI Examples

InvestmentCostReturnROI
Stock purchase$10,000$12,50025%
Marketing campaign$5,000$20,000 revenue300%
College degree (4 yr)$100,000$500K extra lifetime earnings400%
Solar panels$20,000$45,000 savings (25 yr)125%

What is a Good ROI?

ContextGood ROI
Stock market (S&P 500 avg)~10% per year
Real estate8–12% per year
Business investments15–25%+
Marketing campaigns5:1 (500%)

faq.question: What is a good ROI?
faq.answer: It depends on context. Stock market average: ~10%/year (S&P 500 historical). Real estate: 8-12%/year. Business investments: 15-25%+ is typically required. Marketing: 5:1 (500%) is excellent. Any ROI above the risk-free rate (~4-5%) provides value above parking money safely. Always consider the TIME frame — 50% ROI over 10 years (4.1%/year) is less impressive than 20% in 1 year.

faq.question: What are the limitations of ROI?
faq.answer: ROI doesn't account for: TIME (ignores how long the investment takes), RISK (a 10% ROI from a savings account vs. a startup are very different), opportunity cost, or ongoing costs. For time-adjusted returns, use IRR (Internal Rate of Return) or annualized ROI.

faq.question: How do I calculate ROI for a rental property?
faq.answer: Annual ROI = (Annual Net Income / Total Investment) × 100. Purchase $200K + $20K closing. Annual rent $24K − expenses $12K = net $12K. ROI = $12K / $220K = 5.5%. With financing (20% down): $12K / $60K = 20% cash-on-cash ROI.

definition: A measure of financial performance: net income divided by shareholders' equity, showing how effectively a company generates profits from equity capital.
contentHTML:
What is ROE (Return on Equity)?

Return on Equity (ROE) measures how effectively a company uses shareholders' equity to generate profit. It tells investors how much profit is generated for every dollar of equity invested.

Formula

ROE = (Net Income / Shareholders' Equity) × 100

ROE Benchmarks

ROE RangeAssessment
> 20%Excellent — strong value creation
15–20%Good performance
10–15%Average
5–10%Below average
< 5%Poor — may not be creating value above cost of equity

DuPont Analysis (ROE Breakdown)

ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier

ComponentFormulaWhat It Measures
Net MarginNet Income / RevenueProfitability
Asset TurnoverRevenue / Total AssetsEfficiency
Equity MultiplierTotal Assets / EquityLeverage

faq.question: What is the difference between ROI and ROE?
faq.answer: ROI measures return on a specific investment. ROE measures return on shareholders' equity specifically — how well the company uses equity capital to generate profit. ROE is company-wide; ROI can apply to any investment. A company can have high ROE through leverage (debt) — which increases both returns AND risk.

faq.question: Can ROE be too high?
faq.answer: High ROE from excessive leverage (debt) is risky — the DuPont analysis reveals if high ROE comes from high profit margins (good), high asset turnover (good), or high leverage (risky). An ROE of 30% from heavy borrowing is less sustainable than 20% from strong margins. Also, a shrinking equity base (from buybacks or losses) can artificially inflate ROE.

faq.question: How is ROE used by investors?
faq.answer: Investors compare ROE to: cost of equity (ROE should exceed it), industry peers, and historical trends. Consistently high ROE indicates a competitive moat. Warren Buffett famously targets companies with ROE > 15% sustained over 5+ years as a sign of durable competitive advantage.

definition: Weighted Average Cost of Capital — the blended rate a company pays to finance its assets, calculated as the weighted average of debt and equity costs.
contentHTML:
What is WACC?

WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital) is the average rate a company pays to finance its operations, weighted by the proportion of debt and equity in its capital structure. It represents the minimum return a company must earn on existing assets to satisfy creditors and shareholders.

WACC Formula

WACC = (E/V × Re) + (D/V × Rd × (1−T))

VariableMeaning
EMarket value of equity
DMarket value of debt
VE + D (total value)
ReCost of equity
RdCost of debt
TCorporate tax rate

Typical WACC by Industry

IndustryTypical WACC
Utilities4–6%
Real estate5–7%
Healthcare7–10%
Technology8–12%
Startups15–30%+

faq.question: Why is WACC important?
faq.answer: WACC is the hurdle rate for investment decisions. If a project returns 12% but WACC is 10%, it creates value (2% excess return). If the project returns only 8%, it destroys value. WACC is used as the discount rate in DCF (Discounted Cash Flow) valuations — the most common method for valuing companies and projects.

faq.question: How does debt reduce WACC?
faq.answer: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, creating a 'tax shield.' If debt costs 6% and the tax rate is 25%, the after-tax cost of debt is only 6% × (1-0.25) = 4.5%. Since equity cost (~8-12%) is usually higher than after-tax debt cost (~3-5%), adding debt to the capital structure can lower WACC — up to a point. Too much debt increases both Re (equity risk premium) and Rd (default risk), eventually raising WACC.

faq.question: What is cost of equity?
faq.answer: Cost of equity (Re) is estimated using CAPM: Re = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf). Rf = risk-free rate (~4%), β = stock's sensitivity to market movements, (Rm−Rf) = market risk premium (~5-7%). A company with β=1.2: Re = 4% + 1.2×6% = 11.2%. Unlike debt interest, equity cost is implicit (no contractual payment), representing the return shareholders EXPECT.

definition: The total value of a company: market capitalization + total debt − cash and cash equivalents. Used in valuation multiples like EV/EBITDA.
contentHTML:
What is Enterprise Value?

Enterprise Value (EV) represents the total value of a business — what it would cost to acquire the entire company. It includes the value of equity AND debt, minus cash. EV is the most comprehensive measure of a company's true worth.

Enterprise Value Formula

EV = Market Cap + Total Debt − Cash & Cash Equivalents

EV vs Market Cap

MetricWhat It IncludesAnalogy
Market CapShare price × shares outstandingEquity value (your ownership stake)
Enterprise ValueMarket Cap + debt − cashTotal price to buy the whole house (including mortgage)

Example

ItemValue
Share price$50
Shares outstanding10 million
Market cap$500 million
Total debt$200 million
Cash$50 million
Enterprise Value$650 million

faq.question: Why is EV better than market cap for comparisons?
faq.answer: Market cap only reflects equity value. Two companies with the same market cap but different debt levels have very different total values. Company A: $500M market cap, $0 debt = $500M EV. Company B: $500M market cap, $400M debt = $900M EV. Company B is nearly 2× as expensive to acquire. EV-based ratios (EV/EBITDA, EV/Revenue) provide apples-to-apples comparisons regardless of capital structure.

faq.question: Why do we subtract cash from EV?
faq.answer: Cash effectively reduces the buyer's cost. If you acquire a company for $500M but it has $100M cash on hand, the net cost is $400M — you immediately get the cash back. Think of buying a house with $50K cash in the safe: the effective price is the purchase price minus the cash you'll find inside.

faq.question: What are common EV multiples?
faq.answer: EV/EBITDA (most common): 5-8× for mature companies, 10-20× for growth. EV/Revenue: 1-3× for mature, 5-15× for high-growth SaaS. EV/EBIT: similar to EV/EBITDA but includes D&A. The appropriate multiple depends on industry, growth rate, margins, and market conditions. Multiple compression (falling multiples) indicates market pessimism about growth prospects.

definition: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — a measure of a company's core operating profitability before non-operating expenses.
contentHTML:
What is EBITDA?

EBITDA stands for Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization. It measures a company's operating performance by removing the effects of financing decisions, tax jurisdictions, and accounting decisions — providing a cleaner view of core business profitability.

EBITDA Formula

EBITDA = Net Income + Interest + Taxes + Depreciation + Amortization

Or: EBITDA = Operating Income + Depreciation + Amortization

Why EBITDA Matters

What EBITDA RemovesWhy
InterestDepends on capital structure (debt vs equity choice)
TaxesVaries by jurisdiction and tax strategies
DepreciationNon-cash charge based on accounting method
AmortizationNon-cash charge for intangible assets

Business Valuation Multiples

Business TypeTypical EV/EBITDA Multiple
Small business (< $1M EBITDA)3–5×
Mid-market ($1-10M EBITDA)5–8×
Large private company7–12×
SaaS company15–30×
Manufacturing5–8×
Restaurant chain6–10×

faq.question: How is EBITDA used to value a business?
faq.answer: Enterprise Value = EBITDA × industry multiple. A small business with $500K EBITDA at 4× multiple is worth approximately $2 million. The multiple depends on industry, growth rate, customer concentration, competitive moat, and management team. EBITDA is the most common metric used in M&A (mergers and acquisitions) for pricing businesses.

faq.question: Why do some investors dislike EBITDA?
faq.answer: Warren Buffett famously called depreciation 'a very real expense.' Critics argue EBITDA ignores capital expenditures (equipment eventually needs replacement), makes highly leveraged companies look healthier than they are, and can be manipulated through classification of expenses. Free Cash Flow (FCF) is considered a more reliable metric because it accounts for the actual capital needed to maintain the business.

faq.question: What is adjusted EBITDA?
faq.answer: Adjusted EBITDA adds back one-time, non-recurring, or unusual expenses (lawsuit costs, restructuring charges, owner's personal expenses in a private company). It aims to show 'normalized' earnings. In M&A, sellers often present adjusted EBITDA to inflate valuation — buyers should scrutinize every adjustment carefully. Common adjustments: owner's salary above market rate, one-time legal fees, non-recurring COVID impacts.

definition: The percentage of revenue that remains as profit after all expenses. Net profit margin = (Net Income / Revenue) × 100.
contentHTML:
What is Profit Margin?

Profit margin is the percentage of revenue that remains as profit. It is the most fundamental measure of business profitability. There are several types: gross margin, operating margin, and net margin — each including progressively more expenses.

Types of Profit Margin

TypeFormulaWhat It Includes
Gross Margin(Revenue − COGS) / RevenueOnly direct production costs
Operating MarginOperating Income / RevenueCOGS + operating expenses
Net MarginNet Income / RevenueALL costs including interest & taxes

Industry Net Margin Benchmarks

IndustryTypical Net Margin
Software / SaaS15–30%
Financial services15–25%
Healthcare10–20%
Retail3–8%
Grocery1–3%
Airlines2–8%

faq.question: What is a good profit margin?
faq.answer: Depends on industry. A grocery store at 2% net margin can be very healthy (high volume). A SaaS company at 10% may be underperforming (should be 20%+). Compare to your industry, not across industries. For small businesses, target 7-10% net margin as a minimum. Consistently improving margins over time is more important than the absolute number.

faq.question: How do I improve profit margins?
faq.answer: Two levers: increase revenue per unit (pricing power, upsells, premium positioning) or decrease costs (negotiate with suppliers, automate processes, reduce waste, cut unprofitable product lines). Often the highest-impact action is raising prices — a 5% price increase on 50% gross margin products increases margin to 52.5%, a 5% improvement.

faq.question: What is the difference between markup and margin?
faq.answer: Markup = (Price − Cost) / Cost. Margin = (Price − Cost) / Price. A $10 item sold for $15: Markup = 50%, Margin = 33.3%. They always differ (margin < markup for the same product). A 100% markup = 50% margin. This distinction is critical for pricing — many businesses confuse them, leading to lower profitability than expected.

definition: Revenue minus the cost of goods sold (COGS), expressed as a percentage of revenue. Shows the profitability of core product/service before operating expenses.
contentHTML:
What is Gross Margin?

Gross margin is the percentage of revenue remaining after subtracting the cost of goods sold (COGS). It measures how efficiently a company produces and sells its products before operating expenses, interest, and taxes.

Formula

Gross Margin = ((Revenue − COGS) / Revenue) × 100

Industry Benchmarks

IndustryTypical Gross Margin
Software / SaaS70–85%
Pharmaceuticals65–80%
Consumer goods40–60%
Retail25–45%
Restaurant55–65%
Grocery25–30%
Manufacturing25–40%
Automotive15–20%

faq.question: What is included in COGS?
faq.answer: COGS includes DIRECT costs of producing goods: raw materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead, packaging, shipping to warehouse. It does NOT include indirect costs like rent, marketing, administrative salaries, or R&D. For SaaS companies, COGS includes hosting costs, customer support, and third-party licenses. Correctly categorizing COGS is critical for accurate gross margin.

faq.question: What is a good gross margin?
faq.answer: Depends on industry — compare to peers. SaaS: 70%+ (mostly digital delivery). Retail: 30-50%. Manufacturing: 25-40%. Restaurants: food cost ~30% = 70% gross margin on food. A declining gross margin over time is a warning sign — it means your unit economics are deteriorating (rising costs or pricing pressure).

faq.question: How do I improve gross margin?
faq.answer: Increase prices (if market allows), negotiate better supplier terms, improve production efficiency, reduce waste/shrinkage, automate labor-intensive processes, shift product mix toward higher-margin items, and use better inventory management (reduce spoilage, obsolescence). Each 1% improvement in gross margin flows directly to the bottom line.

definition: Current assets minus current liabilities — the capital available for day-to-day operations. Positive working capital indicates short-term financial health.
contentHTML:
What is Working Capital?

Working capital is the difference between a company's current assets and current liabilities. It measures short-term financial health and operational efficiency — the cash available for day-to-day operations.

Formula

Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities

Components

Current AssetsCurrent Liabilities
Cash & cash equivalentsAccounts payable
Accounts receivableShort-term debt
InventoryAccrued expenses
Prepaid expensesCurrent portion of long-term debt
Short-term investmentsTaxes payable

Working Capital Ratio

RatioMeaning
> 2.0Conservative — may be underutilizing assets
1.5–2.0Healthy
1.0–1.5Adequate but watch closely
< 1.0May have trouble meeting short-term obligations

faq.question: Why is working capital important?
faq.answer: Positive working capital means you can pay bills, cover payroll, and fund operations without borrowing. Negative working capital may signal inability to meet short-term obligations — potential insolvency. However, some businesses (like Amazon) operate with negative working capital by design: they collect payment before paying suppliers, using customer money to fund operations.

faq.question: Can too much working capital be bad?
faq.answer: Yes — excessive working capital (ratio > 2.0) may indicate inefficiency: too much cash sitting idle, inventory piling up, or customers paying too slowly. That capital could be invested in growth, paying down debt, or returning to shareholders. The goal is OPTIMAL working capital — enough for operations with efficient use of resources.

faq.question: How do I improve working capital?
faq.answer: Speed up receivables (invoice promptly, offer early-pay discounts). Slow down payables (negotiate longer terms — net 60 vs net 30). Reduce inventory (just-in-time purchasing, better demand forecasting). Convert assets to cash (sell unused equipment). Manage cash flow timing (align inflows with outflows). These working capital optimization strategies can free significant cash without external financing.

definition: A financial leverage ratio comparing total liabilities to shareholders' equity (D/E = Total Debt / Total Equity). Higher ratio = more leveraged.
contentHTML:
What is the Debt-to-Equity Ratio?

The Debt-to-Equity (D/E) ratio compares a company's total debt to shareholders' equity, showing how much of the company's financing comes from debt versus owner investment. It is a key measure of financial leverage and risk.

Formula

D/E Ratio = Total Debt / Shareholders' Equity

Industry Benchmarks

IndustryTypical D/E
Utilities1.0–2.0
Real estate / REITs1.0–3.0
Manufacturing0.5–1.5
Technology0.0–0.5
Retail0.5–1.5
Banks / Financial5.0–15.0 (regulated)

Interpretation

D/E RangeMeaning
0.0–0.5Conservative — low leverage, lower risk
0.5–1.0Moderate leverage — balanced approach
1.0–2.0Significant leverage — higher risk but potentially higher returns
> 2.0Highly leveraged — risky unless industry norm (utilities, RE)

faq.question: Is debt always bad?
faq.answer: No — strategic debt can amplify returns (leverage). If the cost of debt (interest rate) is lower than the return on invested capital, debt creates value. A company borrowing at 5% to invest in projects returning 15% is using debt wisely. The tax deductibility of interest (tax shield) makes debt cheaper than equity in many cases. The key is maintaining debt at sustainable levels with comfortable interest coverage.

faq.question: What D/E ratio is too high?
faq.answer: There's no universal threshold — it depends on industry. A D/E of 2.0 is normal for utilities (stable cash flows support debt) but alarming for a tech startup (volatile revenue). Generally, D/E above 2.0 for non-financial companies signals elevated risk. More important than the absolute ratio: can the company comfortable service its debt? (Interest coverage ratio = EBIT / Interest expense, should be > 3×).

faq.question: How does D/E affect stock valuation?
faq.answer: Higher D/E increases the equity risk premium (shareholders demand higher returns for more leverage risk), raising the cost of equity and potentially lowering valuation multiples. However, moderate debt can increase ROE and reduce WACC (through the tax shield), potentially increasing valuation. The Modigliani-Miller theorem (with taxes) suggests an optimal D/E exists where WACC is minimized and value is maximized.

definition: The net amount of cash moving in and out of a business. Positive cash flow means more money coming in than going out — essential for solvency.
contentHTML:
What is Cash Flow?

Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over a specific period. It represents actual cash received and spent — unlike profit, which includes non-cash items like depreciation. Strong cash flow is essential for paying bills, employees, and investing in growth.

Types of Cash Flow

TypeWhat It IncludesExample
Operating Cash FlowCash from day-to-day operationsCustomer payments, supplier payments, salaries
Investing Cash FlowCash spent on/received from investmentsEquipment purchases, property sales, acquisitions
Financing Cash FlowCash from/to investors and lendersLoans, equity raised, dividends paid, debt repayment

Cash Flow vs Profit

ScenarioProfitCash Flow
Sale made on credit (invoice sent but not paid)Recorded ✓Not received until paid ✗
Depreciation expense ($10K/year)Reduces profit ✗No cash leaves ✓
Loan principal paymentNot an expense ✓Cash leaves ✗
Equipment purchased for $50KNot an expense (capitalized) ✓$50K cash outflow ✗

faq.question: Why is cash flow more important than profit?
faq.answer: A profitable company can go bankrupt if it runs out of cash. You can't pay rent, salaries, or suppliers with profit — you need actual cash. Common scenarios: selling on 90-day payment terms (profit booked but cash delayed), rapid growth requiring inventory investment before sales are collected, and seasonal businesses with uneven revenue. 'Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is king' is the classic saying.

faq.question: What is free cash flow?
faq.answer: Free Cash Flow (FCF) = Operating Cash Flow − Capital Expenditures. It's the cash available after maintaining/expanding the asset base. FCF can be used for dividends, debt repayment, buybacks, or acquisitions. It's considered the most reliable measure of financial health because it's harder to manipulate than earnings. Positive FCF means the business generates more cash than it needs to maintain operations.

faq.question: How do I improve business cash flow?
faq.answer: Invoice immediately and follow up aggressively on receivables. Negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers (net 60 instead of net 30). Reduce inventory levels. Offer early payment discounts (2/10 net 30 — 2% discount for payment within 10 days). Lease equipment instead of buying. Build a cash reserve of 3-6 months operating expenses. Consider invoice factoring for immediate cash.

definition: The present value of all future cash flows from an investment minus the initial cost. NPV > 0 means the investment creates value.
contentHTML:
What is NPV (Net Present Value)?

Net Present Value (NPV) is the difference between the present value of future cash inflows and the present value of cash outflows. It determines whether an investment will generate more value than it costs, accounting for the time value of money.

NPV Formula

NPV = Σ [Cash Flow_t / (1+r)^t] − Initial Investment

Where r = discount rate, t = time period

Decision Rule

NPV ResultDecisionMeaning
NPV > 0Accept ✓Investment creates value
NPV = 0IndifferentEarns exactly the required rate of return
NPV < 0Reject ✗Investment destroys value

Example

Invest $100,000 today. Returns $35,000/year for 4 years. Discount rate = 10%.

YearCash FlowDiscount FactorPresent Value
0-$100,0001.000-$100,000
1$35,0000.909$31,818
2$35,0000.826$28,926
3$35,0000.751$26,296
4$35,0000.683$23,905
NPV$10,945

faq.question: Why is NPV considered the best investment decision tool?
faq.answer: NPV accounts for the time value of money (a dollar today > a dollar tomorrow), considers ALL cash flows over the project's life, and gives a dollar amount of value created. Unlike IRR, it doesn't have multiple solution issues. Unlike payback period, it considers cash flows after payback. It directly measures wealth creation — positive NPV means the investment increases company value by exactly that amount.

faq.question: What discount rate should I use?
faq.answer: Use WACC for corporate projects (typically 8-12%). Use your required rate of return for personal investments. Higher rates for riskier projects (add a risk premium). The discount rate dramatically affects NPV — a $100K project returning $30K/year for 5 years has NPV of $13,724 at 10% but only $3,588 at 14%. Sensitivity analysis (testing multiple rates) is recommended.

faq.question: What is the relationship between NPV and IRR?
faq.answer: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) is the discount rate at which NPV = 0. If IRR > WACC, the project has positive NPV. They usually give the same accept/reject decision but can differ when comparing mutually exclusive projects or when cash flows change signs multiple times. In conflicts, NPV is generally considered more reliable because it measures absolute value created.

definition: The discount rate at which the net present value of all cash flows equals zero. Used to evaluate and compare investment opportunities.
contentHTML:
What is IRR (Internal Rate of Return)?

Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the discount rate at which an investment's Net Present Value (NPV) equals zero. In other words, it is the expected compound annual growth rate an investment will generate. It is one of the most widely used capital budgeting metrics.

Decision Rule

ScenarioDecision
IRR > WACC (or hurdle rate)Accept ✓ (investment creates value)
IRR = WACCIndifferent (breaks even on a risk-adjusted basis)
IRR < WACCReject ✗ (investment destroys value)

IRR Benchmarks

Investment TypeTypical Required IRR
US Treasury bonds4–5% (risk-free baseline)
Corporate bonds5–8%
Public equity market8–10%
Real estate investment10–15%
Private equity15–25%
Venture capital25–50%+

faq.question: How is IRR different from ROI?
faq.answer: ROI is a simple ratio (total gain / cost) that ignores time. IRR is an annualized rate of return that accounts for the timing of cash flows. An investment returning 100% over 10 years has 100% ROI but only ~7.2% IRR. An investment returning 30% in 1 year has both 30% ROI and 30% IRR. For multi-year investments with varying cash flows, IRR gives a much more accurate picture of performance.

faq.question: Can IRR be misleading?
faq.answer: Yes — IRR has limitations: (1) Multiple IRRs for projects with alternating positive/negative cash flows. (2) IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself, which may be unrealistic for high-IRR projects. (3) IRR doesn't account for project size — a 50% IRR on a $1,000 project may be worse than 20% IRR on $1,000,000. Modified IRR (MIRR) addresses the reinvestment assumption. For mutually exclusive projects, NPV is more reliable.

faq.question: What is the difference between IRR and CAGR?
faq.answer: CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) measures the smooth annualized return from beginning to ending value, ignoring intermediate cash flows. IRR accounts for all cash flows at their exact timing. For a simple buy-and-sell investment with no intermediate cash flows, they are identical. But for investments with dividends, contributions, or withdrawals, IRR is more comprehensive.

definition: The time required for an investment to generate enough cash flow to recover the initial investment cost.
contentHTML:
What is Payback Period?

The payback period is the time it takes for an investment to recoup its initial cost from its cumulative cash flows. It answers the simple question: "How long until I get my money back?"

Formula

Payback Period = Initial Investment / Annual Cash Flow (if cash flows are uniform)

Example

YearCash FlowCumulative
0-$50,000-$50,000
1$15,000-$35,000
2$15,000-$20,000
3$15,000-$5,000
4$15,000$10,000 ← payback between year 3-4

Payback = 3 + ($5,000/$15,000) = 3.33 years

Benchmarks

Investment TypeAcceptable Payback
Solar panels (residential)6-10 years
Energy efficiency upgrades2-5 years
Business equipment2-4 years
Marketing campaigns3-12 months
SaaS customer acquisition< 12 months ideal

faq.question: What is a good payback period?
faq.answer: Shorter is better. Most businesses require payback within 2-5 years. High-tech industries may accept 1-2 years (rapid change). Infrastructure investments may accept 5-10+ years. SaaS companies target < 12 months CAC payback. The acceptable period depends on the investment's risk — riskier investments should have shorter payback periods.

faq.question: What are the limitations of payback period?
faq.answer: Payback ignores: (1) Cash flows AFTER payback (a project paying back in 2 years but generating cash for 20 years is undervalued). (2) Time value of money (unless using discounted payback). (3) Profitability — it only measures breakeven speed. Always use payback alongside NPV and IRR for comprehensive analysis.

faq.question: What is discounted payback period?
faq.answer: Discounted payback uses present values of cash flows instead of nominal values, accounting for the time value of money. It's always longer than the simple payback period because discounted cash flows are smaller. Example: $15,000/year at 10% discount has PVs of $13,636, $12,397, $11,270, $10,245... taking longer to reach cumulative breakeven.

definition: The degree to which a company uses fixed costs in its operations. High operating leverage means small revenue changes produce large profit swings.
contentHTML:
What is Operating Leverage?

Operating leverage measures how sensitive a company's operating income is to changes in revenue. High operating leverage means a large proportion of costs are fixed — so small revenue changes cause magnified profit changes.

Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL)

DOL = % Change in Operating Income / % Change in Revenue

Or: DOL = Contribution Margin / Operating Income

High vs Low Operating Leverage

FeatureHigh Operating LeverageLow Operating Leverage
Fixed costsHigh (mostly fixed)Low (mostly variable)
Revenue impactProfit amplified (up AND down)Profit changes proportionally
RiskHigher — losses magnified in downturnsLower — easier to scale down
IndustriesAirlines, software, manufacturing, hotelsConsulting, staffing, retail

Example: DOL = 3

Revenue ChangeOperating Income Change
+10%+30% (great in upswing)
-10%-30% (devastating in downturn)

faq.question: Why does high operating leverage amplify profits?
faq.answer: When most costs are fixed, additional revenue has very low marginal cost — almost all of it drops to profit. A software company with $1M fixed costs and $100K variable costs: at $2M revenue, profit = $900K. At $2.2M (10% increase), profit = $1.1M (22% increase). The fixed cost 'base' means every extra dollar of revenue is nearly pure profit. But it works in reverse — lost revenue still incurs those fixed costs.

faq.question: Is high or low operating leverage better?
faq.answer: Neither is inherently better. High leverage rewards rapid growth (software companies love it) but punishes declines (airlines during COVID). Low leverage provides stability and flexibility (consulting firms can reduce headcount quickly). The best choice depends on revenue stability, growth trajectory, and risk tolerance. Many companies strategically choose their cost structure.

faq.question: How does operating leverage relate to break-even?
faq.answer: High operating leverage = higher break-even point (more fixed costs to cover) but faster profit growth after break-even. Low operating leverage = lower break-even point but slower profit growth. A high-leverage company needs more revenue to break even but earns more profit per additional dollar of revenue once it does.

definition: The total income generated from sales of goods or services before any expenses are deducted. Also called the 'top line' of the income statement.
contentHTML:
What is Revenue?

Revenue (also called sales or turnover) is the total income generated from a company's primary business operations before any expenses are deducted. It is the "top line" of the income statement and the starting point for all profitability calculations.

Types of Revenue

TypeDescriptionExample
Product RevenueIncome from selling physical goodsApple selling iPhones
Service RevenueIncome from providing servicesMcKinsey consulting fees
Recurring RevenueSubscription / repeat revenueNetflix monthly subscriptions
Non-recurring RevenueOne-time incomeSelling a building, licensing deal

Revenue vs Related Terms

TermFormulaMeaning
Gross RevenueTotal sales before any deductions$1,000,000
Net RevenueGross − returns, discounts, allowances$950,000
Gross ProfitNet Revenue − COGS$570,000
Operating IncomeGross Profit − operating expenses$200,000
Net IncomeOperating − interest − taxes$140,000

faq.question: What is the difference between revenue and profit?
faq.answer: Revenue is total income before expenses ('top line'). Profit is what remains after subtracting all expenses ('bottom line'). A company can have $10M revenue and $0 profit (or even losses) if expenses equal or exceed revenue. Revenue shows business scale; profit shows business efficiency. 'Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is king.'

faq.question: What is recurring vs non-recurring revenue?
faq.answer: Recurring revenue comes from ongoing customer relationships (subscriptions, retainers, maintenance contracts) — predictable and highly valued by investors. Non-recurring revenue is one-time (equipment sales, project fees, licensing). SaaS companies emphasize ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) and MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) because predictable revenue is worth higher multiples. A $1M ARR SaaS company may be worth 5-15× ARR.

faq.question: When is revenue recognized?
faq.answer: Under accrual accounting (GAAP/IFRS), revenue is recognized when earned (goods delivered or services rendered) — not necessarily when cash is received. A software company signing a $120K annual contract in January recognizes $10K/month over the year, even if paid upfront. Cash accounting (used by some small businesses) recognizes revenue when cash is received. Mismatched revenue recognition is a common source of accounting fraud.
